Besides, we consider that we have as good a right as anyone to point out a neighbor's faults, particularly when we look at the great contrast between the two national characters — a contrast which, as far as we can tell, you have barely perceived, having never yet considered what sort of opponents you will face in the Athenians, how widely, how absolutely different from yourselves they are. The Athenians are addicted to innovation, and their plans are marked by swiftness in both conception and execution. You have a genius for keeping what you have, combined with a complete lack of invention, and when you are forced to act you never go far enough. They are adventurous beyond their power, daring beyond their judgment, and confident in danger. Your habit is to attempt less than your power justifies, to mistrust even what your own judgment endorses, and to imagine that there is no escape from danger. There is promptness on their side against your delay. They are never at home; you are never away from it. They hope to extend their possessions by being absent; you fear that by advancing you will endanger what you have already secured. They are quick to follow up a success and slow to retreat from a setback. They spend their bodies ungrudgingly in their country's cause, and they jealously husband their intellect to be employed in her service. A scheme not yet carried out is, for them, a positive loss; a successful enterprise is a comparative failure. The gap created by a failed undertaking is quickly filled with fresh hopes — for they alone are able to call something hoped for already won, by the speed with which they act on their decisions. Thus they toil through trouble and danger all the days of their lives, with little chance to enjoy what they have, since they are always busy getting more. Their only idea of a holiday is to do whatever the moment demands, and to them strenuous activity is less of a misfortune than the peace of a quiet life. To put their character in a single word, one might truthfully say that they were born into the world to take no rest themselves and to give none to others.

"Such is Athens, your antagonist. And yet, Lacedaemonians, you still delay, and fail to see that peace lasts longest for those who are no less careful to use their power justly than to make it clear they will not submit to injustice. On the contrary, your idea of fair dealing rests on the principle that, if you do not injure others, you need not put your own fortunes at risk to keep others from injuring you. You could hardly have succeeded in such a policy even with a neighbor like yourselves, and in the present case, as we have just shown, your habits are old-fashioned compared to theirs. The law in politics, as in art, is that improvements always prevail. Fixed customs may be best for undisturbed communities, but the constant demand for action must be met with constantly improved methods. That is how Athens, with her vast experience, has gone further than you down the path of innovation.

"Here at least let your delay end. For the present, help your allies — and Potidæa in particular, as you promised — by a quick invasion of Attica. Do not sacrifice friends and kinsmen to their bitterest enemies, and do not drive the rest of us in despair to seek some other alliance. Such a step would not be condemned either by the gods who received our oaths or by the men who witnessed them. The breach of a treaty cannot be charged against the people whom desertion forces to seek new ties, but against the power that fails to support its confederate. But if you will only act, we will stand by you. It would be unnatural for us to change, and we would never find such a congenial ally. So choose the right course, and try to keep the Peloponnese, under your supremacy, from sinking below the standing it enjoyed under your ancestors."

Such was the speech of the Corinthians. There happened to be Athenian envoys at Lacedaemon at the time on other business. On hearing the speeches they thought they should come forward before the Lacedaemonians. Their intention was not to defend themselves against any of the charges the cities brought against them, but to argue, on a broader view, that the matter was not one to be hastily decided, but demanded further reflection. They also wanted to call attention to Athens' great power, to refresh the memory of the older men and inform the younger ones, in the hope that their words might persuade the Lacedaemonians to prefer peace to war. So they came to the Lacedaemonians and said that they too, if there was no objection, wished to address the assembly. The Lacedaemonians invited them to come forward. The Athenians advanced and spoke as follows:

"The purpose of our mission here was not to argue with your allies, but to handle the business our state sent us on. However, the violence of the outcry against us has persuaded us to come forward — not to answer the charges of the cities (indeed, you are not the judges before whom either we or they could plead), but to keep you from taking the wrong course in matters of great importance by yielding too easily to the persuasions of your allies. We also want to show, in a review of the whole indictment, that we have a fair claim to what we possess, and that our country deserves consideration. We need not refer to the distant past: there we could appeal to tradition, but not to the experience of our audience. We must refer, though, to the Median War and to recent history, even if we are rather tired of bringing this subject up again and again. In our actions during that war, we ran great risks to obtain certain results. You shared in the solid benefits — do not try to rob us of any share in the glory those results may bring us. The story will be told not so much to deprecate hostilities as to bear witness against them, and to show, if you are foolish enough to enter into a struggle with Athens, what sort of opponent she is likely to prove. We assert that at Marathon we stood at the front and faced the barbarian alone. When he came the second time, unable to face him on land, we boarded our ships with all our people and joined the engagement at Salamis. This prevented him from picking off the Peloponnesian states one by one and ravaging them with his fleet, when the sheer number of his vessels would have made any combined defence impossible. The clearest proof of this came from the invader himself. Defeated at sea, he judged that his power was no longer what it had been, and withdrew as quickly as possible with the larger part of his army.

"Such, then, was the outcome, and it was clearly proved that the cause of Hellas hung on her fleet. To that result we contributed three very useful elements: the largest number of ships, the ablest commander, and the most unhesitating patriotism. Our contingent was little less than two-thirds of the whole four hundred ships. The commander was Themistocles, who was chiefly responsible for fighting the battle in the straits — which everyone agrees was the salvation of our cause. That, indeed, was why you welcomed him with honors such as had never been given to any foreign visitor. As for daring patriotism, we had no rivals. Receiving no reinforcements from behind, seeing everything in front of us already subdued, we still had the spirit, after abandoning our city and sacrificing our property — rather than deserting the rest of the league or depriving them of our help by scattering — to throw ourselves into our ships and face the danger, without resenting your failure to come to our aid. We claim, therefore, that we gave you quite as much as we received. You had a stake to fight for: the cities you had left behind were still standing with your homes intact, and you had the prospect of enjoying them again. Your coming was driven as much by fear for yourselves as by concern for us — and you never appeared until we had nothing left to lose. But we left behind a city that was no longer a city, and staked our lives for one that existed only in desperate hope. So we bore our full share in your deliverance as well as our own. If we had imitated others and let fear for our territory drive us into siding with the Mede before you arrived, or if we had let our ruin break our spirit and stop us from boarding our ships, your naval inferiority would have made a sea-battle pointless, and the Mede would have achieved his aims peacefully.

"Surely, Lacedaemonians, neither the patriotism we showed in that crisis nor the wisdom of our counsel earns us such extreme unpopularity with the Hellenes — at least, not unpopularity for our empire. That empire we did not acquire by violence: we acquired it because you were unwilling to see the war against the barbarian through to its end, and because the allies attached themselves to us and spontaneously asked us to take the command. The nature of the case then forced us to bring the empire to its present height, with fear as our principal motive, though honor and interest came in afterwards. At last, when nearly everyone hated us, when some had already revolted and been brought back, when you had ceased to be the friends you once were and had become objects of suspicion and dislike, it no longer seemed safe to give up our empire — especially since all who left us would fall to you. No one can quarrel with a people for making, in matters of enormous risk, the best provision it can for its own interests.

"You, at any rate, Lacedaemonians, have used your supremacy to arrange the states of the Peloponnese to suit yourselves. And if, at the period we were speaking of, you had persevered to the end and incurred hatred in your command, we are sure you would have made yourselves just as galling to the allies, and would have been forced to choose between a strong government and danger to yourselves. So it was no remarkable action on our part, or contrary to the common practice of mankind, if we accepted an empire offered to us and refused to give it up under the pressure of three of the strongest motives — fear, honor, and interest. We did not set the example: it has always been the rule that the weaker should be subject to the stronger. Besides, we believed we deserved our position, and you thought so too, until calculations of interest made you take up the cry of justice — a consideration no one has ever yet brought forward to obstruct his ambition when he had a chance of gaining anything by force. And praise is due to all who, even if they are not so superior to human nature as to refuse dominion, still respect justice more than their position requires them to.

"We imagine that the best demonstration of our moderation would be the conduct of others put in our position. But our fairness, very unreasonably, has earned us condemnation rather than approval. The fact that we hold our contract trials with our allies on equal terms, and have them decided by impartial laws at Athens, has gained us the reputation of being litigious. No one cares to ask why this reproach is not brought against other imperial powers who treat their subjects with less moderation than we do. The reason is that where force can be used, law is not needed. Our subjects, though, are so used to dealing with us as equals that any setback that clashes with their idea of justice — whether it comes from a legal verdict or from the power our empire gives us — makes them forget to be grateful that they are still allowed to keep most of their possessions. They are more vexed at losing a part than they would have been if we had cast law aside from the start and openly indulged our greed. If we had done that, even they would not have disputed that the weaker must give way to the stronger. Men's indignation, it seems, is more excited by a legal wrong than by a violent one: the first looks like being cheated by an equal, the second like being compelled by a superior. They certainly managed to put up with much worse treatment than this from the Mede, and yet they think our rule severe — which is to be expected, since the present always weighs heaviest on the conquered. This much at least is certain. If you were to succeed in overthrowing us and taking our place, you would quickly lose the popularity that fear of us has given you, supposing your present policy at all matches the sample you gave during the brief period of your command against the Mede. Not only is your life at home regulated by rules and institutions incompatible with those of others, but your citizens abroad act neither by these rules nor by those recognized by the rest of Hellas.

"Take your time, then, in forming your resolution, since the matter is of great importance. Do not let yourselves be persuaded by the opinions and complaints of others to bring trouble on yourselves. Consider the enormous influence of accident in war before you commit to it. As war drags on, it generally becomes a matter of chance — chance from which neither of us is exempt, and whose outcome we have to risk in the dark. It is a common mistake when going to war to start at the wrong end: to act first, and only discuss the matter once disaster has struck. But we are not yet so misguided, and as far as we can see, neither are you. So while it is still open to both of us to choose rightly, we ask you not to dissolve the treaty, or to break your oaths, but to settle our differences by arbitration as our agreement provides. Otherwise we call the gods who heard the oaths to witness that, if you begin hostilities, whatever course of action you choose, we will try not to be slow in repelling you."

Such were the words of the Athenians. After the Lacedaemonians had heard the complaints of the allies against the Athenians, and the response of the Athenians, they made everyone withdraw and consulted privately on the question before them. The opinions of the majority all pointed to the same conclusion: the Athenians were open aggressors, and war must be declared at once. But Archidamus, the Lacedaemonian king, who had the reputation of being both wise and moderate, came forward and made the following speech:

"I have not lived this long, Lacedaemonians, without experiencing many wars, and I see those of you who are my own age and will not fall into the common mistake of longing for war out of inexperience or out of a belief in its advantages and its safety. The war you are now debating would, on a sober view of the matter, be one of the greatest scale. In a struggle with Peloponnesians and neighbors our strength is of the same character as theirs, and we can move quickly to different points. But a struggle with a people who live in a distant land, who also have an extraordinary familiarity with the sea, and who are at the highest pitch of preparation in every other department too — with private and public wealth, with ships and horses and heavy infantry, with a population no other Hellenic place can match, and finally with a host of tributary allies — what justifies us in rashly beginning such a war? Where is our confidence that we should rush into it unprepared? Is it in our ships? There we are inferior, and if we are to practice and become a match for them, time will have to pass. Is it in our money? There our deficiency is far greater. We have nothing in our treasury, and we are not ready to contribute it from our private funds. We might place some confidence in our superiority in heavy infantry and population, which will allow us to invade and ravage their lands. But the Athenians have plenty of other land in their empire, and can import what they need by sea. Again, if we try to incite a revolt of their allies, those allies will need a fleet to support them, since most of them are islanders. What kind of war, then, is this to be? Unless we can either beat them at sea or strip them of the revenues that feed their navy, we will gain little but disaster. Meanwhile our honor will be committed to seeing the war through, especially if it comes to be thought that we started the quarrel. Let us never be carried away by the fatal hope that the war can be quickly ended by ravaging their land. I rather fear we may leave it as a legacy to our children — so unlikely is it that the Athenian spirit will be enslaved to its land, or Athenian experience cowed by war.

"Not that I would have you so unfeeling as to let them harm your allies and refrain from exposing their plots. But I urge you not to take up arms at once. Send and remonstrate with them in a tone neither too suggestive of war nor too suggestive of submission, and use the interval to perfect our own preparations. The means will be, first, the acquisition of allies — Hellenic or barbarian, it does not matter, as long as they add to our strength either in ships or in money. I say Hellenic or barbarian, because the odium of such an alliance is canceled, for all of us who like ourselves are targets of Athenian designs, by the law of self-preservation. Secondly, the development of our home resources. If they listen to our embassy, so much the better; if not, after two or three years our position will have been substantially strengthened, and we can then attack them if we think it best. Perhaps by then the sight of our preparations, backed by language equally clear, will have inclined them to submission, while their land is still untouched and their counsels can still aim at preserving advantages not yet destroyed. The only way you can view their land is as a hostage in your hands, and a hostage that is the more valuable the better cultivated it is. You ought to spare it as long as possible, rather than make them desperate and so make them harder to deal with. If we let ourselves be hurried by the complaints of our allies into laying it waste while we are still unprepared, beware that we do not bring deep disgrace and deep difficulty upon the Peloponnese. Complaints — whether of communities or individuals — can be settled. But a war undertaken by a coalition for sectional interests, whose course no one can foresee, does not lend itself easily to a creditable settlement.

"And no one need think it cowardice if a number of confederates pause before attacking a single city. The Athenians have as many allies as we do, and allies that pay tribute. War is not so much a matter of arms as of money, which makes arms of any use. This is truer than ever in a struggle between a land power and a sea power. So let us first provide money, and not let ourselves be swept along by the talk of our allies before we have done so. Since we will bear the largest share of the responsibility for the outcome, good or bad, we also have a right to deliberate calmly about it.

"The slowness and delay that our character is most criticized for need not make you blush. If we undertake the war without preparation, we will only delay its conclusion by hastening its beginning. Moreover, a free and famous city has been ours through all time. The quality they condemn is really nothing but wise moderation. Thanks to it, we alone do not grow insolent in success and give way less than others in misfortune. We are not carried away by the pleasure of being cheered on into risks our judgment condemns. Nor, when annoyed, are we any more convinced by attempts to exasperate us with accusations. We are both warlike and wise, and our sense of order is what makes us so. We are warlike because self-control contains honor as a chief element, and honor contains bravery. And we are wise because we are educated with too little learning to despise the laws, and with too strict a self-control to disobey them. We are brought up not to be too clever in useless matters — such as the knowledge that can give a plausible critique of an enemy's plans in theory but fails to attack them with equal success in practice. Instead we are taught to consider that our enemies' schemes are not unlike our own, and that the accidents of chance cannot be calculated. In practice we always base our preparations against an enemy on the assumption that his plans are sound. It is right to rest our hopes not on a belief in his blunders, but on the soundness of our own arrangements. Nor should we suppose that there is much difference between one man and another — only that the advantage lies with the man reared in the strictest school. These practices, then, that our ancestors have handed down to us, and by which we have always profited, must not be abandoned. We must not be hurried into deciding in the brief space of a single day a question that concerns many lives and fortunes and many cities, and in which honor is deeply involved. We must decide calmly. Our strength is what especially enables us to do this. As for the Athenians, send to them on the matter of Potidæa, send on the matter of the alleged wrongs of the allies — particularly since they are prepared with legal satisfaction. To proceed against one who offers arbitration, as against a wrongdoer, the law forbids. Meanwhile do not neglect preparation for war. This decision will be best for you, and most fearsome to your opponents."
Such were the words of Archidamus. Last came forward Sthenelaidas, one of the ephors for that year, who spoke to the Lacedaemonians as follows:

"The long speech of the Athenians I do not claim to understand. They said a great deal in praise of themselves, but nowhere denied that they are wronging our allies and the Peloponnese. And yet if they behaved well against the Mede then but badly toward us now, they deserve double punishment, for having ceased to be good and for having become bad. We, meanwhile, are the same now as we were then. If we are wise, we will not disregard the wrongs of our allies, or put off until tomorrow the duty of helping those who must suffer today. Others have plenty of money and ships and horses, but we have good allies whom we must not abandon to the Athenians, nor settle the matter by lawsuits and words — for it is anything but in word that we are being harmed. We must give instant and powerful help. And let no one tell us that it is proper for us to deliberate when we are being wronged. Long deliberation is more proper for those who are contemplating wronging others. Vote, then, Lacedaemonians, for war, as the honor of Sparta demands. Do not allow the further growth of Athens, do not betray our allies to ruin, but with the gods on our side let us advance against the aggressors."

With these words, as ephor, he himself put the question to the assembly of the Lacedaemonians. He said he could not tell which was the louder acclamation (their mode of decision is by acclamation, not by voting). In fact he wanted to make them declare their opinion openly and so increase their ardor for war. So he said: "All Lacedaemonians who think the treaty has been broken and that Athens is guilty, leave your seats and go there" — pointing to a certain place — "all who hold the opposite opinion, there." They stood up and divided, and those who held that the treaty had been broken were in a decided majority. They then summoned the allies and told them that in their opinion Athens had committed injustice, but that they wished to convene all the allies and put it to a vote, so that they might make war, if so decided, on a common resolution. Having thus gained their point, the delegates returned home at once. The Athenian envoys followed a little later, once they had finished the business of their mission. This decision of the assembly, judging that the treaty had been broken, was made in the fourteenth year of the thirty years' truce that had been entered into after the affair of Euboea.

The Lacedaemonians voted that the treaty had been broken and that war must be declared, not so much because they were persuaded by the arguments of the allies as because they feared the growth of Athenian power, seeing most of Hellas already subject to them.

chapters.title: Book 1, Chapter 4 — From the end of the Persian to the beginning of the Peloponnesian War—The Progress from Supremacy to Empire
paragraphs: Here is how Athens came to find herself in the position from which her power grew. After the Medes had been beaten by sea and land by the Hellenes and had retreated from Europe, and after those who had fled with their ships to Mycale had been wiped out, Leotychides, king of the Lacedaemonians and commander of the Hellenes at Mycale, went home with the allies from the Peloponnese. The Athenians and the allies from Ionia and the Hellespont, who had now revolted from the King, stayed behind and laid siege to Sestos, which the Medes still held. They wintered before it, and when the barbarians evacuated the place they took it; after that they sailed back from the Hellespont to their own cities. Meanwhile, with the barbarian gone from their country, the Athenian people at once began bringing back their children, their wives, and what property they had left from the places where they had stored them, and prepared to rebuild their city and their walls. Only isolated stretches of the wall were still standing, and most of the houses were in ruins, though a few remained — the ones the Persian grandees had used as quarters.

When the Lacedaemonians realized what the Athenians were planning, they sent an embassy to Athens. They themselves would have preferred not to see Athens or any other city behind walls, but they were acting mainly at the urging of their allies, who were alarmed by the strength of her newly built navy and the courage she had shown in the war against the Medes. They asked the Athenians not only to refrain from building walls of their own, but also to join them in tearing down such walls as still stood in cities outside the Peloponnese. The real point of this advice — the suspicion of Athens behind it — was not openly stated. The line they took was that if the barbarian invaded a third time, he would have no strong base of operations such as Thebes had given him before, and that the Peloponnese would be enough for everyone, both as a refuge and as a launching point. After the Lacedaemonians had said this, the Athenians, on Themistocles’ advice, dismissed them at once, with the answer that envoys would be sent to Sparta to discuss the question. Themistocles told the Athenians to send him off to Lacedaemon as fast as possible, but to delay sending his colleagues, even after they had been chosen, until the wall had been raised to a height from which it could be defended. In the meantime the whole population of the city — the Athenians, their wives, and their children — was to work on the wall, sparing no building, public or private, that could be of any use; everything was to be torn down for materials. After giving these orders and adding that he would handle everything else at Sparta himself, he set off. When he arrived at Lacedaemon he did not seek an audience with the authorities but stalled and made excuses. Whenever any member of the government asked him why he had not appeared in the assembly, he said he was waiting for his colleagues, who had been held up in Athens by some piece of business; he expected them shortly, and was puzzled they were not yet there. At first the Lacedaemonians believed him, out of friendship for him; but as more and more people kept arriving from Athens, all clearly stating that the work was going on and was already getting some height, they could no longer disbelieve it. Aware of this, Themistocles told them that rumours were unreliable and should not be trusted: they should send respectable people from Sparta to inspect, men whose report could be trusted. They duly dispatched them. Themistocles secretly sent word to the Athenians to detain these men as far as possible without putting them under open restraint, and not to let them go until he and his colleagues had returned home. For his colleagues — Abronichus, son of Lysicles, and Aristides, son of Lysimachus — had now joined him, with the news that the wall was high enough; and he was afraid that once the Lacedaemonians heard the truth, they might refuse to release them. So the Athenians detained the envoys as Themistocles had instructed, and Themistocles got his audience with the Lacedaemonians and at last told them outright that Athens was now fortified well enough to protect its inhabitants; that any embassy the Lacedaemonians or their allies wished to send to Athens in future should approach her on the assumption that she could tell what was in her own and the common interest. When the Athenians had decided to abandon their city and take to their ships, they had taken that dangerous step without consulting Sparta; and on every other occasion when they had deliberated together with the Lacedaemonians, their judgement had proved second to none. They now thought it right that their city should have a wall, and that this would be more to the advantage of both the Athenian citizens and the Hellenic confederacy as a whole; for without equal military strength it was impossible to contribute equal or fair counsel to the common cause. Either, he pointed out, all members of the confederacy should be without walls, or what Athens had just done should be accepted as right.

The Lacedaemonians showed no open anger toward the Athenians at what they heard. The embassy, it seems, had been intended not to obstruct, but to guide the policy of the Athenian government; and Spartan feeling at that time was very friendly toward Athens because of the patriotism she had shown in the struggle against the Mede. Still, the failure of their wishes could not help causing them quiet annoyance. The envoys of each state went home without making any complaint.

In this way the Athenians walled their city in a short time. To this day the work shows the haste with which it was done: the foundations are laid with stones of every kind, in some places not dressed or fitted but placed just as the workers brought them up; many columns from tombs and sculptured stones were built in along with the rest. The bounds of the city were extended at every point of the circumference, so they laid hands on everything in their hurry. Themistocles also persuaded them to finish the walls of Piraeus, which had been begun earlier during his year as archon. He was drawn both by the natural quality of a site that had three harbours, and by the great advantage Athens would gain in becoming a sea power. He was the first to dare tell them to stick to the sea, and at once began laying the foundations of the empire. It was on his advice, too, that they built the walls of Piraeus to the thickness still visible today — the stones being brought up by two wagons meeting each other. Between the two faces there was no rubble or mortar, but great squared blocks of stone, fitted together and clamped on the outside with iron and lead. About half the height he intended was finished. His idea was that, by their size and thickness, the walls would keep off any attack: he reckoned a small garrison of invalids could defend them, and the rest could be freed for service in the fleet. The fleet got most of his attention. He saw, I think, that an approach by sea was easier for the King’s army than one by land; and he considered Piraeus more valuable than the upper city. In fact he was always advising the Athenians that, should the day come when they were hard pressed by land, they should go down into Piraeus and defy the world with their fleet. So the Athenians completed their wall and started their other buildings as soon as the Mede had withdrawn.

Meanwhile Pausanias, son of Cleombrotus, was sent out from Lacedaemon as commander-in-chief of the Hellenes, with twenty ships from the Peloponnese. He sailed with thirty Athenian ships and a number of other allies. They mounted an expedition against Cyprus and subdued most of the island, and afterwards against Byzantium, which was held by the Medes, and forced it to surrender. This happened while the Spartans were still in command. But Pausanias’ violence had already begun to alienate the Hellenes, particularly the Ionians and the recently liberated populations. They turned to the Athenians and asked them, as kinsmen, to take the lead and put a stop to any violence on Pausanias’ part. The Athenians accepted the offer and resolved both to check him and to settle everything else as their own interests seemed to require. In the meantime the Lacedaemonians recalled Pausanias to investigate the reports they had received. Numerous and serious accusations had been brought against him by Hellenes arriving in Sparta; and to all appearances he had played the role of an autocrat more than that of a general. As it happened, his recall coincided with the moment when the hatred he had aroused had driven the allies, except for the soldiers from the Peloponnese, to desert him and side with the Athenians. On his return to Lacedaemon he was censured for his private acts of oppression but acquitted on the heaviest charges and pronounced not guilty — though it should be noted that the charge of Medism was one of the principal counts and, by all appearances, one of the best founded. The Lacedaemonians did not, however, restore him to his command. They sent out Dorkis and a few others with a small force, who found the allies no longer willing to grant them the supremacy. Seeing this, they left, and the Lacedaemonians did not send anyone to replace them. They feared that those who went out would deteriorate as Pausanias had; besides, they wanted to be done with the Median War, and they were satisfied that the Athenians were up to the position and at that moment friendly toward themselves.

The Athenians, having thus succeeded to the supremacy by the voluntary act of the allies, who hated Pausanias, decided which cities were to contribute money against the barbarian and which were to contribute ships. Their stated aim was to retaliate for what they had suffered by ravaging the King’s country. It was now that the office of “Treasurers for Hellas” was first established by the Athenians. These officials received the tribute, as the contributed money was called. The tribute was first fixed at four hundred and sixty talents. The common treasury was at Delos, and the congresses were held in the temple. Their supremacy began with allies who were independent and acted on the resolutions of a common congress. It was marked by the following undertakings, in war and in administration, during the interval between the Median War and the present war — against the barbarian, against their own rebellious allies, and against the Peloponnesian powers they came into contact with on various occasions. My reason for relating these events, and for venturing on this digression, is that this stretch of history has been left out by all my predecessors, who confined themselves either to Hellenic history before the Median War or to the Median War itself. Hellanicus did touch on these events in his Athenian history, but he is rather brief and not accurate in his dates. Besides, the history of these events explains the growth of the Athenian empire.

First the Athenians besieged and captured Eion on the Strymon from the Medes, and enslaved the inhabitants, under the command of Cimon, son of Miltiades. Next they enslaved Scyros, the island in the Aegean, which had a Dolopian population, and colonized it themselves. Then came a war against Carystus, in which the rest of Euboea remained neutral; it ended in surrender on terms. After this Naxos left the confederacy, war followed, and after a siege she was forced back in. This was the first instance of the agreement being broken by the subjugation of an allied city — a precedent the rest followed in the order circumstances dictated. Of all the causes of defection, the chief was failure to keep up the tribute and the supply of vessels, and failure to perform service. The Athenians were severe and exacting, and they made themselves offensive by applying the screw to men who were not used to and not really inclined to any continuous effort. In other respects too the Athenians were no longer the popular leaders they had been at the start. If they took more than their fair share of the work, it was correspondingly easy for them to bring back into line any state that tried to leave the confederacy. The allies had themselves to blame for this. Most of them, wanting to avoid service, arranged to pay their share of the cost in money instead of in ships, so as not to leave home. So while Athens was building up her navy on the funds they contributed, a revolt would always find them without resources or experience for war.

Next come the actions by land and sea at the river Eurymedon between the Athenians and their allies and the Medes, when the Athenians won both battles on the same day under the command of Cimon, son of Miltiades, and captured and destroyed the entire Phoenician fleet of two hundred ships. Some time later came the defection of the Thasians, caused by disagreements about the trading posts on the opposite coast of Thrace and about the mine the Thasians held. Sailing against Thasos, the Athenians defeated them at sea and made a landing on the island. Around the same time they sent out ten thousand settlers — their own citizens and allies — to colonize the place then called Ennea Hodoi, or Nine Ways, now Amphipolis. They managed to take Ennea Hodoi from the Edonians, but on advancing into the interior of Thrace they were cut off at Drabescus, a town of the Edonians, by the assembled Thracians, who saw the settlement at Ennea Hodoi as an act of war. Meanwhile the Thasians, beaten in the field and besieged, appealed to Lacedaemon, asking her to help by invading Attica. Without informing Athens, Sparta promised to do so and intended to, but was prevented by the earthquake — which was followed by the secession of the Helots, and of the Thuriats and Aethaeans of the Perioeci, to Ithome. Most of the Helots were descendants of the old Messenians enslaved in the famous war, so all of them came to be called Messenians. So while the Lacedaemonians were tied up in a war against the rebels at Ithome, the Thasians, in the third year of the siege, came to terms with the Athenians by tearing down their walls, surrendering their ships, agreeing to pay the demanded sums at once and tribute thereafter, and giving up their possessions on the mainland together with the mine.

Meanwhile the Lacedaemonians, finding the war against the rebels at Ithome likely to drag on, called for help from their allies, and especially from the Athenians, who came in some force under the command of Cimon. The reason for the urgent summons was the Athenians’ reputed skill in siege operations: a long siege had taught the Lacedaemonians how deficient they were in this art, otherwise they would have taken the place by assault. The first open quarrel between Lacedaemonians and Athenians arose out of this expedition. When assault failed to take Ithome, the Lacedaemonians, alarmed by the enterprising and revolutionary character of the Athenians, and regarding them besides as alien in stock, began to fear that, if they stayed, they might be tempted by the besieged at Ithome to attempt some political change. So they dismissed them — them alone of all the allies — without admitting their suspicion, simply saying they no longer needed them. But the Athenians realized that they had been sent away not for the more honourable of the two reasons, but because of the suspicions held against them. They left deeply offended, conscious that they had done nothing to deserve such treatment from the Lacedaemonians. The instant they got home they broke off the alliance against the Mede and allied themselves with Sparta’s enemy, Argos; each party taking the same oaths and making the same alliance with the Thessalians.

Meanwhile the rebels at Ithome, unable to keep up a ten years’ resistance any longer, surrendered to Lacedaemon. The terms were that they should leave the Peloponnese under safe conduct and never set foot in it again: anyone caught there afterwards was to become the slave of his captor. It should be noted that the Lacedaemonians had an old oracle from Delphi telling them to release the suppliant of Zeus at Ithome. So they went out with their children and their wives and were received by Athens — out of the hatred she now felt for the Lacedaemonians — and settled at Naupactus, which Athens had recently taken from the Ozolian Locrians. The Athenians gained another addition to their confederacy in the Megarians, who left the Lacedaemonian alliance, irritated by a war over boundaries that Corinth had forced on them. The Athenians occupied Megara and Pegae, and built the Megarians their long walls from the city to Nisaea, in which they placed an Athenian garrison. This was the main reason the Corinthians conceived such a deadly hatred of Athens.

Meanwhile Inaros, son of Psammetichus, a Libyan king of the Libyans on the Egyptian border, with his headquarters at Marea, the town above Pharos, caused almost the whole of Egypt to revolt from King Artaxerxes. Putting himself at the head of the revolt, he invited the Athenians to come to his aid. Abandoning a Cyprian expedition on which they happened to be engaged with two hundred ships of their own and their allies, the Athenians arrived in Egypt, sailed up from the sea into the Nile, took control of the river and of two-thirds of Memphis, and then turned to attacking the remaining third, which is called White Castle. Inside it were Persians and Medes who had taken refuge there, and Egyptians who had not joined the revolt.

Meanwhile the Athenians, making a landing from their fleet at Haliae, were engaged by a force of Corinthians and Epidaurians, and the Corinthians won. Afterwards the Athenians fought the Peloponnesian fleet off Cecruphalia, and the Athenians won. Then war broke out between Aegina and Athens. There was a great sea battle off Aegina between Athenians and Aeginetans, each side helped by their allies; the Athenians won, taking seventy of the enemy’s ships. They landed and began a siege of the country under the command of Leocrates, son of Stroebus. At this the Peloponnesians, wanting to help the Aeginetans, threw three hundred heavy infantry — who had previously been serving with the Corinthians and Epidaurians — into Aegina. Meanwhile the Corinthians and their allies seized the heights of Geraneia and marched down into the Megarid, in the belief that with so large an Athenian force absent in Aegina and Egypt, Athens would be unable to help the Megarians without lifting the siege of Aegina. But the Athenians, instead of moving the army at Aegina, raised a force from the old men and the boys who had been left in the city, and marched into the Megarid under the command of Myronides. After a drawn battle with the Corinthians, the two sides parted, each thinking they had won. The Athenians had rather the better of it, and after the Corinthians left they set up a trophy. Stung by taunts from the elders in their city, the Corinthians made their preparations and about twelve days later came back and set up their own trophy as victors. Sallying out from Megara, the Athenians cut off the party that was setting up the trophy, then engaged and defeated the rest. As the beaten army retreated, a sizeable detachment, hard pressed by the pursuers and missing the road, blundered into a piece of private land surrounded by a deep trench, with no way out. Knowing the place, the Athenians sealed off the front with heavy infantry, posted light troops in a ring around it, and stoned to death every man inside. This was a heavy blow to Corinth. The bulk of her army continued its retreat home.

About this time the Athenians began to build the long walls down to the sea, one toward Phalerum and one toward Piraeus. Meanwhile the Phocians made an expedition against Doris, the original homeland of the Lacedaemonians, which contained the towns of Boeum, Kitinium, and Erineum. They had taken one of these towns when the Lacedaemonians, under Nicomedes, son of Cleombrotus, who was acting for King Pleistoanax, son of Pausanias, still a minor, came to the Dorians’ aid with fifteen hundred heavy infantry of their own and ten thousand of their allies. After forcing the Phocians to give back the town on terms, they began their retreat. The route by sea, across the Crissaean Gulf, exposed them to being cut off by the Athenian fleet; the route across Geraneia hardly seemed safe either, since the Athenians held Megara and Pegae. The pass was difficult and was always guarded by the Athenians; and on this occasion the Lacedaemonians had information that the Athenians meant to dispute their passage. So they decided to remain in Boeotia and consider which route was safest. They had another reason for staying as well: a party in Athens had quietly encouraged them, hoping to put an end to the democracy and the building of the Long Walls. Meanwhile the Athenians marched against them with their full levy, a thousand Argives, and contingents from the rest of their allies. Altogether they were fourteen thousand strong. The march was prompted by the impression that the Lacedaemonians were at a loss how to get through, and also by suspicion of an attempt to overthrow the democracy. Some cavalry from their Thessalian allies also joined the Athenians, but these went over to the Lacedaemonians during the battle.

The battle was fought at Tanagra in Boeotia. After heavy losses on both sides, victory went to the Lacedaemonians and their allies. After moving into the Megarid and cutting down the fruit trees, the Lacedaemonians went home across Geraneia and the isthmus. Sixty-two days after the battle, the Athenians marched into Boeotia under the command of Myronides, defeated the Boeotians at Oenophyta, and became masters of Boeotia and Phocis. They dismantled the walls of Tanagra, took a hundred of the richest men of the Opuntian Locrians as hostages, and finished their own long walls. After this came the surrender of the Aeginetans to Athens on terms: they tore down their walls, gave up their ships, and agreed to pay tribute in future. The Athenians sailed round the Peloponnese under Tolmides, son of Tolmaeus, burnt the Lacedaemonian dockyard, captured Chalcis, a Corinthian town, and in a landing at Sicyon defeated the Sicyonians in battle.

Meanwhile the Athenians and their allies were still in Egypt, going through every kind of fortune in war. At first the Athenians were masters of Egypt, and the King sent Megabazus, a Persian, to Lacedaemon with money to bribe the Peloponnesians to invade Attica and so draw the Athenians off from Egypt. When this made no progress and the money was simply being wasted, he recalled Megabazus with what was left of it and sent Megabuzus, son of Zopyrus, a Persian, with a large army into Egypt. Coming by land, he defeated the Egyptians and their allies in a battle, drove the Hellenes out of Memphis, and finally penned them up on the island of Prosopitis, where he besieged them for a year and a half. At last he drained the canal, diverting the water into another channel, leaving their ships high and dry and joining most of the island to the mainland. He then marched across on foot and took the place. So after six years of war the Hellenic enterprise came to ruin. Of all that great force, a few got through Libya safely to Cyrene, but most perished. Egypt returned to its subjection to the King, except for Amyrtaeus, the king in the marshes, whom they could not capture because of the size of the marsh — the marshmen also being the most warlike of the Egyptians. Inaros, the Libyan king who alone had set off the Egyptian revolt, was betrayed, captured, and crucified. Meanwhile a relieving squadron of fifty ships had set out from Athens and the rest of the confederacy for Egypt. They put in at the Mendesian mouth of the Nile, with no idea of what had happened. Attacked on the land side by the troops, and from the sea by the Phoenician navy, most of the ships were destroyed; the few survivors got away by retreat. Such was the end of the great Athenian and allied expedition to Egypt.

Meanwhile Orestes, son of Echecratidas, the Thessalian king, an exile from Thessaly, persuaded the Athenians to restore him. Taking with them the Boeotians and Phocians, their allies, the Athenians marched on Pharsalus in Thessaly. They became masters of the country, but only in the immediate area of the camp; beyond that they could not go for fear of the Thessalian cavalry. They failed to take the city or to achieve any of the other aims of the expedition, and went home with Orestes, having accomplished nothing. Not long after this, a thousand Athenians embarked in the ships at Pegae — Pegae, remember, was now theirs — and sailed along the coast to Sicyon under the command of Pericles, son of Xanthippus. Landing at Sicyon and defeating the Sicyonians who came out to meet them, they immediately picked up the Achaeans, sailed across, and marched against and laid siege to Oeniadae in Acarnania. Failing to take it, they returned home.

Three years later a truce was made between the Peloponnesians and the Athenians for five years. Released from war within Hellas, the Athenians made an expedition to Cyprus with two hundred ships of their own and their allies, under Cimon’s command. Sixty of these were detached to Egypt at the request of Amyrtaeus, the king in the marshes; the rest laid siege to Kitium, from which, however, they were forced to withdraw because of Cimon’s death and a shortage of provisions. Sailing off Salamis in Cyprus, they fought the Phoenicians, Cyprians, and Cilicians by land and sea, and, victorious on both elements, they returned home together with the squadron that had come back from Egypt. After this the Lacedaemonians launched a sacred war, gained control of the temple at Delphi, and put it in the hands of the Delphians. As soon as they had withdrawn, the Athenians marched out, took the temple, and put it in the hands of the Phocians.

Some time later, when Orchomenus, Chaeronea, and certain other places in Boeotia were in the hands of Boeotian exiles, the Athenians marched against these hostile places with a thousand Athenian heavy infantry and contingents from the allies, under the command of Tolmides, son of Tolmaeus. They took Chaeronea, enslaved the inhabitants, left a garrison, and started home. On the way they were attacked at Coronea by the Boeotian exiles from Orchomenus, joined by some Locrians, Euboean exiles, and others of the same persuasion. They were defeated; some were killed, others taken prisoner. The Athenians evacuated the whole of Boeotia by a treaty providing for the recovery of the men. The exiled Boeotians returned, and along with the rest regained their independence.

This was soon followed by the revolt of Euboea from Athens. Pericles had already crossed over to the island with an Athenian army when news reached him that Megara had revolted, that the Peloponnesians were about to invade Attica, and that the Athenian garrison had been cut off by the Megarians, except for a few who had taken refuge in Nisaea. The Megarians had let the Corinthians, Sicyonians, and Epidaurians into the town before they revolted. Meanwhile Pericles brought his army back from Euboea as fast as he could. After this the Peloponnesians invaded Attica as far as Eleusis and Thrius, ravaging the country under the command of King Pleistoanax, son of Pausanias, and went home without advancing further. The Athenians then crossed back to Euboea under Pericles and subdued the whole island. All but Histiaea was settled by agreement; the Histiaeans they expelled from their homes and took the territory for themselves.

Not long after their return from Euboea, they made a thirty-year truce with the Lacedaemonians and their allies, giving up the posts they held in the Peloponnese — Nisaea, Pegae, Troezen, and Achaia. In the sixth year of the truce, war broke out between the Samians and the Milesians over Priene. Beaten in the war, the Milesians came to Athens with loud complaints against the Samians. They were joined by certain private individuals from Samos itself, who wanted to overturn the government. So the Athenians sailed to Samos with forty ships, set up a democracy there, took fifty boys and as many men from the Samians as hostages, lodged them on Lemnos, left a garrison on the island, and went home. But some of the Samians had not stayed on the island; they had fled to the mainland. Coming to an arrangement with the most powerful of those left in the city, and forming an alliance with Pissuthnes, son of Hystaspes, then satrap of Sardis, they got together a force of seven hundred mercenaries and crossed over to Samos under cover of night. Their first move was to rise against the commons, most of whom they secured; their next was to steal back their hostages from Lemnos. Then they openly revolted, handed the Athenian garrison and its commanders over to Pissuthnes, and immediately prepared an expedition against Miletus. The Byzantines also revolted with them.

As soon as the Athenians heard the news, they sailed against Samos with sixty ships. Sixteen of these were sent off to Caria to watch for the Phoenician fleet, and to Chios and Lesbos to call up reinforcements, and so never engaged. The remaining forty-four, under Pericles and nine colleagues, gave battle off the island of Tragia to seventy Samian ships — twenty of them transports — that were sailing from Miletus. Victory went to the Athenians. Reinforced afterwards by forty ships from Athens and twenty-five from Chios and Lesbos, the Athenians landed, gained the upper hand on land, and surrounded the city with three walls. It was blockaded from the sea as well. Meanwhile Pericles took sixty ships from the blockading squadron and hurried off to Caunus and Caria, on news that the Phoenician fleet was coming to help the Samians; in fact Stesagoras and others had left the island with five ships to bring it. In the meantime the Samians made a sudden sally, fell on the camp, which they found unfortified, destroyed the lookout vessels, and engaged and defeated those that were being launched to meet them. They held command of their own waters for fourteen days and brought in and out whatever they pleased. But on Pericles’ return, they were shut up again. Fresh reinforcements then arrived: forty ships from Athens under Thucydides, Hagnon, and Phormio; twenty under Tlepolemus and Anticles; and thirty from Chios and Lesbos. After a brief attempt at fighting, the Samians, unable to hold out, surrendered after a nine-month siege on terms — they tore down their walls, gave hostages, surrendered their ships, and agreed to pay the cost of the war by instalments. The Byzantines also agreed to be subjects again, as before.

chapters.title: Book 1, Chapter 5 — Second Congress at Lacedaemon—Preparations for War and Diplomatic Skirmishes—Cylon—Pausanias—Themistocles
paragraphs: After this, though not many years later, we at last come to what has already been described—the affairs of Corcyra and Potidæa, and the events that served as the pretext for the present war. All these actions of the Hellenes against each other and against the barbarian took place in the fifty-year interval between the retreat of Xerxes and the beginning of the present war. During this interval the Athenians succeeded in placing their empire on a firmer footing and raised their own home power to a very great height. The Lacedaemonians, fully aware of it, opposed it only briefly, but stayed inactive most of the time, being from of old slow to go to war except under pressure of necessity, and at this moment hampered by wars at home. Eventually the growth of Athenian power could no longer be ignored, and their own confederacy became the object of its encroachments. Then they felt they could endure it no longer; the time had come to throw themselves heart and soul against the hostile power and break it, if they could, by starting the present war. Although the Lacedaemonians had already decided that the treaty was broken and the Athenians were guilty, they still sent to Delphi and asked the god whether it would go well with them if they went to war; and, as the story goes, they received the answer that if they put their whole strength into the war, victory would be theirs, and the promise that he himself would be with them, whether invoked or not. Still they wanted to summon their allies again and take a vote on whether to make war. After the ambassadors from the confederates had arrived and a congress had been convened, they all spoke their minds, most of them denouncing the Athenians and demanding that the war begin. The Corinthians in particular. They had already, on their own account, been canvassing the cities one by one to induce them to vote for war, fearing it might come too late to save Potidæa. They were present on this occasion as well, came forward last, and made the following speech:

“Fellow allies, we can no longer accuse the Lacedaemonians of having failed in their duty: they have not only voted for war themselves, but have assembled us here for that purpose. We say their duty, because supremacy has its duties. Beyond fairly administering private interests, leaders are required to show special care for the common welfare, in return for the special honours accorded them by everyone in other ways. As for ourselves, all who have already had dealings with the Athenians need no warning to be on guard against them. The states more inland, off the main lines of communication, should understand that if they fail to support the coast powers, the result will be to hurt the transit of their produce for export and the receipt in exchange of their imports from the sea. They must not weigh what is now said as if it had nothing to do with them. They should expect that the sacrifice of the powers on the coast will one day be followed by the extension of the danger to the interior, and recognise that their own interests are deeply involved in this discussion. For these reasons they should not hesitate to exchange peace for war. Wise men remain quiet so long as they are not injured; brave men abandon peace for war when they are injured, returning to an understanding when a favourable opportunity arises. They are neither intoxicated by their success in war nor disposed to put up with an injury for the sake of the delightful tranquillity of peace. To falter for the sake of such delights is, if you remain inactive, the quickest way to lose the very repose you cling to; while to form extravagant ambitions out of success in war is to forget how hollow the confidence is that elates you. For if many ill-conceived plans have succeeded thanks to the still greater stupidity of an opponent, many more, apparently well-laid, have ended in disgrace. The confidence with which we form our schemes is never fully justified in carrying them out; speculation is safe, but when it comes to action, fear causes failure.

“To apply these rules to ourselves: if we are now kindling war, it is under the pressure of injury, with adequate grounds of complaint; and once we have punished the Athenians, we will desist in good time. We have many reasons to expect success—first, superiority in numbers and in military experience; and second, our general and unvarying obedience in carrying out orders. The naval strength they possess we shall raise from our existing resources and from the funds at Olympia and Delphi. A loan from these will let us seduce their foreign sailors by offering higher pay. For the power of Athens is more mercenary than national; ours will not be exposed to the same risk, since its strength lies more in men than in money. A single defeat at sea is in all likelihood their ruin: should they hold out, in that case there will be all the more time for us to train ourselves in naval matters; and once we have reached equality in skill, we hardly need ask whether we shall surpass them in courage. The advantages we have by nature they cannot acquire by training; while their superiority in skill must be removed by our practice. The money required for these objects shall be supplied by our contributions: nothing could be more monstrous than the suggestion that, while their allies never tire of contributing for their own enslavement, we should refuse to spend on vengeance and self-preservation the treasure which by such refusal we shall forfeit to Athenian rapacity and see used for our own ruin.

“We also have other ways of carrying on the war, such as inciting their allies to revolt—the surest way to deprive Athens of the revenues that are the source of her strength—and establishing fortified positions in their country, along with various operations that cannot be foreseen at present. War, more than anything, proceeds least by definite rules, and draws chiefly on its own resources to meet emergencies; in such cases the side that faces the struggle and keeps its temper best meets with most security, and the side that loses its temper meets with corresponding disaster. Let us also reflect that if it were merely a matter of disputes over territory between rival neighbours, it might be borne; but here we have an enemy in Athens that is a match for our whole coalition, and more than a match for any of its members. So unless, as a body and as individual peoples and individual cities, we make a unanimous stand against her, she will easily conquer us, divided and in detail. That conquest, terrible as it may sound, would mean nothing less than slavery, plain and simple—a word the Peloponnese cannot even hear whispered without disgrace, or watch so many states abused by one without disgrace. The opinion would be either that we deserved it, or that we put up with it from cowardice and were proving degenerate sons by failing to secure even the freedom our fathers gave to Hellas, and by allowing the establishment of a tyrant state in Hellas, even though within our own individual states we think it our duty to put down sole rulers. We do not see how this conduct can be cleared of three of the gravest failings—want of sense, want of courage, and want of vigilance. We do not suppose that you have taken refuge in that contempt for an enemy which has proved fatal in so many cases—a feeling which, from the numbers it has ruined, has come to be called not contemptuous but contemptible.

“There is no advantage in reflections on the past beyond what serves the present. For the future we must provide by holding what we have and redoubling our efforts. It is hereditary to us to win virtue as the fruit of labour, and you must not change the habit, even if you have a slight advantage in wealth and resources. It is not right that what was won in want should be lost in plenty. We must boldly advance to war for many reasons: the god has commanded it and promised to be with us, and the rest of Hellas will all join in the struggle, partly from fear, partly from interest. You will not be the first to break a treaty which the god, by counselling us to go to war, judges already broken; rather you will be supporting a treaty that has been outraged. Treaties are broken not by resistance but by aggression.

“Your position, then, from any angle you view it, will amply justify you in going to war; and we recommend this step in the interests of all, remembering that identity of interest is the surest of bonds, whether between states or individuals. Do not delay to assist Potidæa, a Dorian city besieged by Ionians, which is a complete reversal of the natural order, nor to assert the freedom of the rest. We can wait no longer when waiting can only mean immediate disaster for some of us, and—if it becomes known that we have conferred but do not dare to protect ourselves—the same disaster in the near future for the rest. Do not delay, fellow allies, but, convinced of the necessity of the crisis and the wisdom of this counsel, vote for war—undeterred by its immediate terrors and looking beyond to the lasting peace that will succeed it. Out of war peace gains fresh stability, but to refuse to abandon repose for war is no surer way of avoiding danger. We must believe that the tyrant city established in Hellas has been established against all alike, with a programme of universal empire, part of it already achieved, the rest in contemplation. Let us then attack it, reduce it, and win future security for ourselves and freedom for the Hellenes who are now enslaved.”

Such were the words of the Corinthians. Having now heard everyone, the Lacedaemonians took the vote of all the allied states present, in turn, great and small alike; and the majority voted for war. With this decided, it was still impossible to begin at once, since they were not prepared. It was resolved that each state should procure the necessary means and that there should be no delay. Yet, despite the time taken up by the necessary arrangements, less than a year passed before Attica was invaded and the war openly begun.

This interval was spent sending embassies to Athens with complaints, in order to obtain as good a pretext for war as possible if she paid no attention to them. The first Lacedaemonian embassy ordered the Athenians to drive out the curse of the goddess. Its history is as follows. In former generations there was an Athenian named Cylon, an Olympic victor, of good birth and powerful position, who had married a daughter of Theagenes, a Megarian, then tyrant of Megara. This Cylon was inquiring at Delphi when the god told him to seize the Acropolis of Athens at the grand festival of Zeus. Accordingly, getting a force from Theagenes and persuading his friends to join him, when the Olympic festival in the Peloponnese came around, he seized the Acropolis with the intention of making himself tyrant. He thought this was the grand festival of Zeus and an occasion fitting for an Olympic victor. Whether the festival meant was in Attica or elsewhere was a question he never thought about, and the oracle did not offer to settle it. The Athenians too have a festival called the grand festival of Zeus Meilichios, the Gracious—the Diasia. It is celebrated outside the city, where the whole people sacrifice not real victims but a number of bloodless offerings peculiar to the country. Convinced he had picked the right time, he made the attempt. As soon as the Athenians realised what was happening, they flocked in from the country, every man of them, and sat down to besiege the citadel. As time wore on, weary of the labour of blockade, most of them went home, leaving responsibility for the watch to the nine archons, with full powers to settle everything as they saw fit. It must be remembered that at that time most political functions were carried out by the nine archons. Meanwhile Cylon and his besieged companions were in distress for want of food and water. Cylon and his brother managed to escape; but the rest, hard pressed and some even dying of hunger, sat as suppliants at the altar in the Acropolis. The Athenians on guard duty, when they saw them at the point of death in the temple, raised them up on the understanding that no harm would be done to them, led them out, and killed them. Some who took refuge as they passed by at the altars of the awful goddesses were dispatched on the spot. From this deed the men who killed them were called accursed and guilty against the goddess—they and their descendants. These cursed ones were driven out by the Athenians, then driven out again by Cleomenes of Lacedaemon and an Athenian faction; the living were expelled and the bones of the dead taken up; thus they were cast out. Even so they came back later, and their descendants are still in the city.

This, then, was the curse the Lacedaemonians ordered them to drive out. They were primarily motivated, as they pretended, by concern for the honour of the gods. But they also knew that Pericles, son of Xanthippus, was connected with the curse on his mother’s side, and they thought his banishment would substantially advance their designs on Athens. Not that they really expected to succeed; rather they meant to create prejudice against him in the eyes of his countrymen, suggesting that the war would be partly caused by his bad luck. For he was the most powerful man of his time and the leading Athenian statesman, and he opposed the Lacedaemonians on every issue, refused all concessions, and constantly urged the Athenians on toward war.

The Athenians retorted by ordering the Lacedaemonians to drive out the curse of Taenarus. The Lacedaemonians had once raised some Helot suppliants from the temple of Poseidon at Taenarus, led them away, and killed them; for which they believe the great earthquake at Sparta was retribution. The Athenians also ordered them to drive out the curse of the goddess of the Brazen House, the history of which is as follows. After Pausanias the Lacedaemonian had been recalled by the Spartans from his command in the Hellespont (this was his first recall), and had been tried by them and acquitted, he was not sent out again in any official capacity. He took a galley of Hermione on his own responsibility, without Lacedaemonian authority, and arrived as a private person in the Hellespont. He came ostensibly for the Hellenic war, but really to pursue his intrigues with the King, which he had begun before his recall, ambitious to rule over Hellas. The circumstance that first allowed him to put the King in his debt and to begin the whole design was this. Some of the King’s connections and kinsmen had been captured at Byzantium when the city was taken from the Medes, when Pausanias was first there after the return from Cyprus. He sent these prisoners off to the King without the knowledge of the rest of the allies, with the cover story that they had escaped. He arranged this with the help of Gongylus, an Eretrian, whom he had put in charge of Byzantium and the prisoners. He also gave Gongylus a letter for the King, the contents of which—as was later discovered—were as follows: “Pausanias, the general of Sparta, eager to do you a favour, sends you these prisoners of war. I propose also, with your approval, to marry your daughter and to make Sparta and the rest of Hellas subject to you. I believe I am able to do this, with your cooperation. So if any of this pleases you, send a trusty man to the sea through whom we may carry on our future correspondence.”

That was all that was revealed in the writing, and Xerxes was pleased with the letter. He sent off Artabazus, son of Pharnaces, to the sea with orders to replace Megabates, the previous governor of the satrapy of Daskylion, and to send across as quickly as possible a letter—entrusted to him—for Pausanias at Byzantium; to show him the royal seal; and to carry out any commission Pausanias might give him on the King’s business with all care and fidelity. Artabazus, on arriving, carried out the King’s orders and sent over the letter, which contained this answer: “Thus says King Xerxes to Pausanias. For the men whom you have saved for me from across the sea from Byzantium, an obligation is laid up for you in our house, recorded forever; and with your proposals I am well pleased. Let neither night nor day stop you from diligently performing any of your promises to me. Let neither cost in gold nor in silver hold them back, nor any number of troops, wherever their presence is needed; but with Artabazus, an honourable man whom I send you, boldly advance my objects and yours, in whatever way most serves the honour and interest of us both.”

Already held in high honour among the Hellenes as the hero of Plataea, Pausanias, after receiving this letter, became prouder than ever, and could no longer live in the usual style. He went out of Byzantium in Median dress, was attended on his march through Thrace by a bodyguard of Medes and Egyptians, kept a Persian table, and was quite unable to contain his intentions; he betrayed in trifles what his ambition meant one day to enact on a grander scale. He also made himself difficult to approach, and showed so violent a temper to everyone, without exception, that no one could come near him. This indeed was the principal reason the confederacy went over to the Athenians.

This conduct, when it came to the ears of the Lacedaemonians, occasioned his first recall. After his second voyage out in the Hermione ship, without their orders, he gave further proofs of similar behaviour. Besieged and expelled from Byzantium by the Athenians, he did not return to Sparta. News came that he had settled at Colonae in the Troad and was intriguing with the barbarians, and that his stay there was for no good purpose. The ephors, no longer hesitating, sent him a herald and a scytale with orders to accompany the herald or be declared a public enemy. Anxious above all to avoid suspicion, and confident he could quash the charge with money, he returned a second time to Sparta. At first thrown into prison by the ephors—whose powers allow them to do this even to the King—he soon compromised the matter, was released, and offered himself for trial to anyone who wished to bring an inquiry against him.

The Spartans had no tangible proof against him—neither his enemies nor the nation at large had any of that indisputable kind required for the punishment of a member of the royal family who was at that moment in high office. He was regent for his first cousin King Pleistarchus, son of Leonidas, who was still a minor. But by his contempt for the laws and his imitation of the barbarians, he gave grounds for much suspicion that he was discontented with the established order. All the occasions on which he had departed in any way from the regular customs were reviewed, and it was remembered that he had taken it upon himself to have inscribed on the tripod at Delphi—dedicated by the Hellenes as the first-fruits of the spoils of the Medes—the following couplet:
The Mede defeated, great Pausanias raised This monument, that Phœbus might be praised.

At the time the Lacedaemonians had erased the couplet at once and inscribed instead the names of the cities that had aided in the overthrow of the barbarian and dedicated the offering. Pausanias was considered to have been guilty of a grave offence here—one which, interpreted in the light of the attitude he had since taken, gained a new significance and seemed perfectly in keeping with his current schemes. They were also informed that he was even intriguing with the Helots; and so it was, for he promised them freedom and citizenship if they would join him in revolt and help him carry out his plans to the end. Even now, mistrusting the evidence even of the Helots themselves, the ephors would not consent to take any decisive step against him, in line with their regular custom toward fellow Spartans—to be slow to take any irrevocable decision in the case of a Spartan citizen without indisputable proof. At last, it is said, the man who was to carry the latest letter to Artabazus for the King, an Argilian and once Pausanias’s favourite and most trusted servant, turned informer. Alarmed by the thought that none of the previous messengers had ever returned, he had counterfeited the seal so that, if he were mistaken in his suspicions, or if Pausanias asked to make some change, he would not be found out. He undid the letter and found the postscript he had suspected—an order to put him to death.

On being shown the letter, the ephors now felt more certain. Still they wanted to hear Pausanias commit himself with their own ears. So the man went, by appointment, to Taenarus as a suppliant, and there built himself a hut divided in two by a partition; behind it he hid some of the ephors and let them hear the whole matter plainly. Pausanias came to him and asked the reason for his suppliant position; the man reproached him with the order he had written about him, and one by one declared all the rest of the circumstances—how, although Pausanias had never yet brought him into any danger when he was employed as agent between him and the King, he was now to be rewarded with death like the rest of his servants. Admitting all this and telling him not to be angry about it, Pausanias gave him his pledge to raise him up from the temple, and begged him to set off as quickly as possible and not to delay the business in hand.

The ephors listened carefully and then left, taking no action for the moment. Now that they had certainty at last, they were preparing to arrest him in the city. It is reported that, just as he was about to be arrested in the street, he saw from the face of one of the ephors what he was coming for; another, too, made him a secret signal, betraying it out of kindness. Setting off at a run for the temple of the goddess of the Brazen House, the precinct of which was nearby, he managed to take sanctuary before they could seize him, and entered a small chamber that formed part of the temple, to keep out of the weather, where he lay still. The ephors, having lost ground in the pursuit, afterwards took the roof off the chamber and, having made sure he was inside, shut him in, barricaded the doors, and stayed in front of the place, reducing him by starvation. When they found he was on the point of dying, just as he was, in the chamber, they brought him out of the temple while the breath was still in him, and as soon as he was outside he died. They were going to throw him into the Kaiadas, where they cast criminals, but in the end they decided to bury him somewhere nearby. Later the god at Delphi ordered the Lacedaemonians to move the tomb to the place of his death—where he now lies in the consecrated ground, as an inscription on a monument declares—and, since what had been done was a curse on them, to give back two bodies instead of one to the goddess of the Brazen House. So they had two bronze statues made and dedicated them as a substitute for Pausanias. The Athenians retorted by telling the Lacedaemonians to drive out what the god himself had pronounced a curse.

To return to the Medism of Pausanias. Material was found in the course of the inquiry that implicated Themistocles. The Lacedaemonians accordingly sent envoys to the Athenians, demanding that he be punished as Pausanias had been. The Athenians agreed. As it happened, however, he had been ostracised, and, while living at Argos, was in the habit of visiting other parts of the Peloponnese. So the Athenians sent agents along with the Lacedaemonians, who were ready to join the pursuit, with instructions to take him wherever they found him. But Themistocles got wind of their intentions and fled from the Peloponnese to Corcyra, which was under obligations to him. The Corcyraeans claimed they could not risk sheltering him at the cost of offending Athens and Lacedaemon, and they conveyed him over to the continent opposite. Pursued by officers who hung on every report of his movements, at a loss where to turn, he was forced to stop at the house of Admetus, the Molossian king, though they were not on friendly terms. Admetus happened not to be at home, but his wife, to whom he made himself a suppliant, instructed him to take their child in his arms and sit down by the hearth. Soon afterwards Admetus came in, and Themistocles told him who he was and begged him not to take revenge on a Themistocles in exile for any opposition his requests might have met from Themistocles at Athens. He was now far too low for revenge; retaliation was honourable only between equals.
