That offer having been refused, they were now, they considered, by the loyalty of their intention, released from the covenant; and having, as they considered, suffered evil at the Plataeans' hands, they brought them in again one by one and asked each the same question — whether they had done the Lacedaemonians and their allies any service in the war — and on their saying that they had not, took them out and killed them, all without exception. The number of Plataeans massacred this way was not less than two hundred, with twenty-five Athenians who had shared in the siege. The women were taken as slaves. The city the Thebans gave for about a year to some political emigrants from Megara and to the surviving Plataeans of their own party to inhabit, and afterwards razed it to the ground from the very foundations. Onto the precinct of Hera they built an inn two hundred feet square, with rooms all around above and below, using for this purpose the roofs and doors of the Plataeans. Of the rest of the materials in the wall, the brass and the iron, they made couches which they dedicated to Hera, for whom they also built a stone chapel a hundred feet square. The land they confiscated and let out on a ten-year lease to Theban occupiers. The adverse attitude of the Lacedaemonians in the whole Plataean affair was mainly adopted to please the Thebans, who were thought to be useful in the war then raging. Such was the end of Plataea, in the ninety-third year after she became the ally of Athens.

Meanwhile, the forty Peloponnesian ships that had gone to the relief of the Lesbians — and which we left flying across the open sea, pursued by the Athenians — were caught in a storm off Crete, and scattering from there, made their way to the Peloponnese, where they found at Cyllene thirteen Leucadian and Ambraciot galleys, with Brasidas, son of Tellis, lately arrived as counsellor to Alcidas. The Lacedaemonians, on the failure of the Lesbian expedition, had resolved to strengthen their fleet and sail to Corcyra, where a revolution had broken out, in order to arrive there before the twelve Athenian ships at Naupactus could be reinforced from Athens. Brasidas and Alcidas accordingly began their preparations.

The Corcyraean revolution began with the return of the prisoners taken in the sea-fights off Epidamnus. The Corinthians had released these men, nominally on the security of eight hundred talents put up by their proxeni, but in reality on their undertaking to bring Corcyra over to Corinth. These men set to work canvassing each of the citizens and intriguing to detach the city from Athens. On the arrival of an Athenian and a Corinthian vessel, with envoys on board, a conference was held in which the Corcyraeans voted to remain allies of the Athenians according to their agreement, but to be friends of the Peloponnesians, as they had been before. Meanwhile, the returned prisoners brought Peithias, a volunteer proxenus of the Athenians and leader of the commons, to trial on the charge of enslaving Corcyra to Athens. Acquitted, he retorted by charging five of the wealthiest of their number with cutting stakes in the ground sacred to Zeus and Alcinous, the legal penalty being a stater for each stake. They were convicted, and the amount of the penalty being very large, they seated themselves as suppliants in the temples to be allowed to pay it by instalments. But Peithias, who was one of the senate, persuaded that body to enforce the law; on which the accused, made desperate by the law, and also learning that Peithias intended, while still a member of the senate, to persuade the people to conclude a defensive and offensive alliance with Athens, banded together, armed with daggers, and suddenly bursting into the senate, killed Peithias and sixty others — senators and private citizens. Only a few of Peithias's party took refuge in the Athenian galley, which had not yet sailed.

After this outrage, the conspirators summoned the Corcyraeans to an assembly and said that what they had done would turn out for the best, and would save them from being enslaved by Athens. For the future, they moved that neither party should be received unless they came peacefully in a single ship, any larger number being treated as enemies. They made this motion and forced it through, and at once sent off envoys to Athens to justify what had been done and to dissuade the refugees there from any hostile proceedings that might lead to a reaction.

On the arrival of the embassy, the Athenians arrested the envoys and all who listened to them as revolutionists, and lodged them in Aegina. Meanwhile, a Corinthian galley arrived in the island with Lacedaemonian envoys, and the dominant Corcyraean party attacked the commons and defeated them in battle. Night coming on, the commons took refuge in the Acropolis and the higher parts of the city, and concentrated themselves there, also holding the Hyllaic harbour. Their adversaries occupied the marketplace, where most of them lived, and the harbour next to it, facing the mainland.

The next day passed in skirmishes of little importance, each party sending out into the country to offer freedom to the slaves and to invite them to join them. The mass of the slaves answered the appeal of the commons; their opponents were reinforced by eight hundred mercenaries from the mainland.

After a day's interval, hostilities resumed, with victory remaining with the commons, who had the advantage in numbers and position, the women also valiantly assisting them by pelting tiles from the houses and supporting the melee with a fortitude beyond their sex. Toward dusk, the oligarchs, in full rout and fearing that the victorious commons might assault and take the arsenal and put them to the sword, set fire to the houses around the marketplace and the lodging-houses to bar their advance, sparing neither their own nor those of their neighbours. Much of the merchants' stock was consumed, and the city would have risked total destruction had a wind come up to help the flame by blowing on it. Hostilities now ceased; both sides kept quiet, passing the night on guard, while the Corinthian ship slipped out to sea on the victory of the commons, and most of the mercenaries crossed secretly over to the mainland.

The next day the Athenian general Nicostratus, son of Diitrephes, came up from Naupactus with twelve ships and five hundred Messenian heavy infantry. He at once tried to bring about a settlement and persuaded the two parties to agree to bring to trial ten of the ringleaders — who promptly fled — while the rest were to live in peace, coming to terms with each other and entering into a defensive and offensive alliance with the Athenians. This arranged, he was about to sail away when the leaders of the commons induced him to leave them five of his ships, so as to make their adversaries less inclined to make a move, while they would man and send with him an equal number of their own. He had no sooner consented than they began enrolling their enemies for the ships; and these, fearing that they might be sent off to Athens, seated themselves as suppliants in the temple of the Dioscuri. An attempt by Nicostratus to reassure them and persuade them to rise proved unsuccessful, and the commons, taking this as a pretext, armed themselves, alleging the refusal of their adversaries to sail with them as proof of the hollowness of their intentions. They took their arms out of their houses and would have killed some whom they fell in with, if Nicostratus had not prevented it. The rest of the party, seeing what was going on, seated themselves as suppliants in the temple of Hera, no fewer than four hundred in number; until the commons, fearing they might adopt some desperate resolution, induced them to rise and conveyed them over to the island in front of the temple, where provisions were sent across to them.

At this stage in the revolution, on the fourth or fifth day after the removal of the men to the island, the Peloponnesian ships arrived from Cyllene, where they had been stationed since their return from Ionia. There were fifty-three of them, still under the command of Alcidas, but with Brasidas also on board as his adviser. Dropping anchor at Sybota, a harbour on the mainland, at daybreak they made sail for Corcyra.

The Corcyraeans, in great confusion and alarm at the state of things in the city and at the approach of the invader, at once set about equipping sixty vessels, which they sent out, as fast as they were manned, against the enemy, despite the Athenians recommending that they let them sail out first and follow themselves afterwards with all their ships together. As their vessels came up to the enemy in this straggling fashion, two immediately deserted; in others the crews were fighting among themselves, and there was no order in anything that was done. So the Peloponnesians, seeing their confusion, placed twenty ships to oppose the Corcyraeans, and ranged the rest against the twelve Athenian ships, among which were the two vessels Salaminia and Paralus.

While the Corcyraeans, attacking without judgment and in small detachments, were already crippled by their own misconduct, the Athenians, afraid of the numbers of the enemy and of being surrounded, did not venture to attack the main body or even the centre of the division opposed to them. Instead they fell on its wing and sank one vessel; after which the Peloponnesians formed in a circle, and the Athenians rowed round them and tried to throw them into disorder. Seeing this, the division opposed to the Corcyraeans, fearing a repeat of the disaster of Naupactus, came up to support their friends, and the whole fleet now bore down united on the Athenians, who retired before it, backing water and withdrawing as leisurely as possible to give the Corcyraeans time to escape, while the enemy was kept occupied. Such was the character of this sea-fight, which lasted until sunset.

The Corcyraeans now feared that the enemy would follow up their victory and sail against the town and rescue the men in the island, or strike some other equally decisive blow; so they carried the men over again to the temple of Hera, and kept guard over the city. The Peloponnesians, however, although victorious in the sea-fight, did not venture to attack the town, but took the thirteen Corcyraean vessels they had captured and sailed back with them to the mainland from which they had set out. The next day they likewise refrained from attacking the city, although the disorder and panic were at their height, and although Brasidas, it is said, urged Alcidas, his superior officer, to attack; instead they landed at the promontory of Leukimme and laid waste the country.

Meanwhile the commons in Corcyra, still in great fear of the fleet attacking them, came to a parley with the suppliants and their friends in order to save the town, and persuaded some of them to go on board the ships, of which they still manned thirty, against the expected attack. But the Peloponnesians, after ravaging the country until midday, sailed away, and toward nightfall were informed by beacon signals of the approach of sixty Athenian vessels from Leucas, under the command of Eurymedon, son of Thucles, which had been sent off by the Athenians on news of the revolution and of the fleet under Alcidas being about to sail for Corcyra.

The Peloponnesians accordingly set off in haste at once for home by night, coasting along the shore, and to avoid being seen rounding the Isthmus of Leucas, they hauled their ships across it and so departed. The Corcyraeans, made aware of the approach of the Athenian fleet and the departure of the enemy, brought the Messenians from outside the walls into the town, and ordered the fleet they had manned to sail round into the Hyllaic harbour. While it was doing so, they killed any of their enemies they could lay hands on, dispatching afterwards, as they landed them, those whom they had persuaded to go on board the ships. Next they went to the sanctuary of Hera and persuaded about fifty men to take their trial, and condemned them all to death. The mass of the suppliants who refused to do this, on seeing what was happening, killed each other there in the consecrated ground; some hanged themselves on the trees, and others destroyed themselves in whatever way they could. During the seven days that Eurymedon stayed with his sixty ships, the Corcyraeans were busy butchering those of their fellow citizens whom they regarded as their enemies. Although the crime alleged was an attempt to overturn the democracy, some were also killed for private hatred, others by their debtors because of the money owed to them. Death thus raged in every shape; and, as usually happens at such times, there was no length to which violence did not go: sons were killed by their fathers, suppliants were dragged from the altar or slain on it, and some were even walled up in the temple of Dionysus and died there.

So bloody was the course of the revolution, and the impression it made was the greater because it was one of the first to occur. Later, one may say, the whole Hellenic world was convulsed; struggles being everywhere made by the popular leaders to bring in the Athenians, and by the oligarchs to bring in the Lacedaemonians. In peace there would have been neither the pretext nor the wish to make such an invitation; but in war, with an alliance always at the disposal of either faction for the harm of their adversaries and their own corresponding advantage, opportunities for bringing in the foreigner were never wanting to the revolutionary parties. The sufferings that revolution brought on the cities were many and terrible, such as have occurred and always will occur as long as the nature of mankind remains the same — though in a more severe or milder form, varying in their symptoms with the variety of cases. In peace and prosperity, states and individuals have better sentiments, because they are not suddenly confronted with imperious necessities; but war takes away the easy supply of daily wants, and so proves a rough master that brings most men's characters down to the level of their fortunes. Revolution thus ran its course from city to city, and the places it reached last, having heard what had been done before, carried the refinement of their inventions to still greater excess, as shown in the cunning of their enterprises and the atrocity of their reprisals. Words had to change their ordinary meaning and to take that which was now given them. Reckless audacity came to be considered the courage of a loyal ally; prudent hesitation, specious cowardice; moderation, a cloak for unmanliness; ability to see all sides of a question, an inability to act on any. Frantic violence became the attribute of manliness; cautious plotting, a justifiable means of self-defence. The advocate of extreme measures was always trustworthy; his opponent a man to be suspected. To succeed in a plot was to have a shrewd head; to detect one, a still shrewder. But to try to provide against having to do either was to break up your party and to fear your adversaries. In short, to forestall an intending criminal, or to suggest the idea of a crime where it was not yet there, was equally commended — until even blood became a weaker tie than party, from the superior readiness of those united by the latter to dare anything without reserve. Such associations had not in view the blessings derived from established institutions, but were formed by ambition for their overthrow; and the confidence of their members in each other rested less on any religious sanction than on shared complicity in crime. The fair proposals of an adversary were met by the stronger of the two with jealous precautions, not with a generous confidence. Revenge also was held of more account than self-preservation. Oaths of reconciliation, offered on either side only to meet an immediate difficulty, held good only as long as no other weapon was at hand; but when opportunity offered, he who first ventured to seize it and catch his enemy off guard thought this perfidious vengeance sweeter than an open one, since, considerations of safety apart, success by treachery won him the palm of superior intelligence. Indeed it is generally the case that men are readier to call rogues clever than simpletons honest, and are as ashamed of being the second as they are proud of being the first. The cause of all these evils was the lust for power arising from greed and ambition; and from these passions proceeded the violence of parties once engaged in contention. The leaders in the cities, each side equipped with the fairest professions — on the one side the cry of political equality of the people, on the other a moderate aristocracy — sought prizes for themselves in those public interests they pretended to cherish, and, recoiling from no means in their struggles for ascendancy, engaged in the direst excesses. In their acts of vengeance they went to even greater lengths, not stopping at what justice or the good of the state demanded, but making the party caprice of the moment their only standard, and invoking with equal readiness the condemnation of an unjust verdict or the authority of the strong arm to glut the animosities of the hour. So religion was in honour with neither party, but the use of fair phrases to arrive at guilty ends was in high reputation. Meanwhile the moderate part of the citizens perished between the two, either for not joining in the quarrel, or because envy would not suffer them to escape.

Thus every form of iniquity took root in the Hellenic countries because of the troubles. The ancient simplicity into which honour so largely entered was laughed out and vanished; and society became divided into camps in which no man trusted his fellow. To put an end to this, there was no promise that could be depended on, nor oath that could command respect; but all parties, dwelling rather on the hopelessness of a permanent state of things in their calculations, were more intent on self-defence than capable of confidence. In this contest, the blunter wits were most successful. Apprehensive of their own deficiencies and of the cleverness of their antagonists, they feared to be worsted in debate and surprised by the combinations of their more versatile opponents, and so at once boldly had recourse to action; while their adversaries, arrogantly assuming that they would know in time and that it was unnecessary to secure by action what policy afforded, often fell victims to their lack of precaution.

Meanwhile Corcyra gave the first example of most of the crimes referred to: the reprisals exacted by the governed who had never experienced equitable treatment or indeed anything but insolence from their rulers — when their hour came; the iniquitous resolves of those who desired to be rid of their accustomed poverty, and ardently coveted their neighbours' goods; and lastly, the savage and pitiless excesses into which men who had begun the struggle, not in a class but in a party spirit, were hurried by their ungovernable passions. In the confusion into which life was now thrown in the cities, human nature, always in revolt against the law and now its master, gladly showed itself ungoverned in passion, above respect for justice, and the enemy of all superiority; for revenge would not have been set above religion, nor gain above justice, had it not been for the fatal power of envy. Indeed, men too often take it upon themselves, in the prosecution of their revenge, to set the example of doing away with those general laws to which all alike can look for salvation in adversity, instead of allowing them to subsist against the day of danger when their aid may be required.

While the revolutionary passions were thus displaying themselves for the first time in the factions of Corcyra, Eurymedon and the Athenian fleet sailed away. After this, some five hundred Corcyraean exiles who had succeeded in escaping took some forts on the mainland, and, becoming masters of the Corcyraean territory across the water, made this their base for plundering their countrymen on the island, and did so much damage as to cause a severe famine in the town. They also sent envoys to Lacedaemon and Corinth to negotiate their restoration, but meeting with no success, afterwards collected boats and mercenaries and crossed over to the island, about six hundred in all. They burned their boats, so as to have no hope except in becoming masters of the country, went up to Mount Istone, and fortifying themselves there began to harass those in the city and gained command of the country.

At the close of the same summer the Athenians sent twenty ships under the command of Laches, son of Melanopus, and Charoeades, son of Euphiletus, to Sicily, where the Syracusans and Leontines were at war. The Syracusans had for allies all the Dorian cities except Camarina — these had been included in the Lacedaemonian confederacy from the start of the war, though they had not taken any active part in it. The Leontines had Camarina and the Chalcidian cities. In Italy the Locrians were for the Syracusans, the Rhegians for their Leontine kinsmen. The allies of the Leontines now sent to Athens and appealed to their ancient alliance and to their Ionian origin to persuade the Athenians to send them a fleet, since the Syracusans were blockading them by land and sea. The Athenians sent it on the plea of their common descent, but in reality to prevent the exportation of Sicilian corn to the Peloponnese and to test the possibility of bringing Sicily into subjection. Accordingly they established themselves at Rhegium in Italy, and from there carried on the war together with their allies.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 11 — Year of the War—Campaigns of Demosthenes in Western Greece—Ruin of Ambracia
paragraphs: Summer was now over. The following winter the plague struck the Athenians a second time. It had never entirely left them, but there had been a noticeable lull in its ravages. The second visit lasted no less than a year, the first having lasted two; and nothing distressed the Athenians or weakened their power more. No fewer than four thousand four hundred heavy infantry in the ranks died of it, three hundred cavalry, and an unknown number of the common multitude. At the same time came the numerous earthquakes in Athens, Euboea, and Boeotia, particularly at Orchomenus in Boeotia.

The same winter the Athenians in Sicily and the Rhegians, with thirty ships, made an expedition against the islands of Aeolus, which cannot be invaded in summer because of the lack of water. These islands are held by the Liparaeans, a Cnidian colony, who live in one of them — Lipara, which is not large — and from this as their headquarters work the rest, Didyme, Strongyle, and Hiera. On Hiera the people in those parts believe that Hephaestus has his forge, from the amount of flame they see it send out by night and the smoke by day. These islands lie off the coast of the Sicels and Messenians and were allies of the Syracusans. The Athenians laid waste their land, and as the inhabitants would not submit, sailed back to Rhegium. So the winter ended, and with it the fifth year of this war of which Thucydides was the historian.

The next summer the Peloponnesians and their allies set out to invade Attica under the command of Agis, son of Archidamus. They got as far as the Isthmus, but with numerous earthquakes occurring, they turned back without invading. About the same time as these earthquakes were so frequent, the sea at Orobiae in Euboea retreated from the existing line of coast and then returned in a huge wave, swept over a great part of the town, and withdrew, leaving some of it still under water; what was once land is now sea. Those of the inhabitants who could not run up to higher ground in time perished. A similar inundation happened at Atalanta, the island off the Opuntian Locrian coast, carrying away part of the Athenian fort and wrecking one of two ships drawn up on the beach. At Peparethus too the sea retreated a little, but no flood followed; an earthquake threw down part of the wall, the town hall, and a few other buildings. The cause of this phenomenon, in my opinion, must be sought in the earthquake. At the point where its shock has been most violent, the sea is driven back, and then, recoiling suddenly with redoubled force, causes the inundation. Without an earthquake I do not see how such a thing could happen.

During the same summer the various belligerents in Sicily carried on different operations: the Sicilians among themselves, and the Athenians and their allies. I will, however, confine myself to the actions in which the Athenians took part, choosing the most important. After the death of the Athenian general Charoeades, killed by the Syracusans in battle, Laches was left in sole command of the fleet, which he now directed in concert with the allies against Mylae, a town belonging to the Messenians. Two Messenian battalions in garrison at Mylae set an ambush for the party landing from the ships, but were routed with great slaughter by the Athenians and their allies, who then assaulted the fortification and forced them to surrender the acropolis and march with them against Messina. This town also submitted afterwards on the approach of the Athenians and their allies, and gave hostages and all other securities required.

The same summer the Athenians sent thirty ships round the Peloponnese under Demosthenes, son of Alcisthenes, and Procles, son of Theodorus, and sixty more, with two thousand heavy infantry, against Melos under Nicias, son of Niceratus. They wanted to reduce the Melians, who, although islanders, refused to be subjects of Athens or even to join her confederacy. The devastation of their land did not bring them to terms, so the fleet weighed from Melos and sailed to Oropus in the territory of Graea. Landing at nightfall, the heavy infantry started at once from the ships by land for Tanagra in Boeotia, where they were met, by prearranged signal, by the whole levy from Athens, under Hipponicus, son of Callias, and Eurymedon, son of Thucles. They encamped, and after spending that day ravaging the territory of Tanagra, stayed there for the night. The next day, after defeating those of the Tanagraeans who came out against them and some Thebans who had come up to help them, they took some arms, set up a trophy, and withdrew — the troops to the city, the rest to the ships. Nicias, with his sixty ships, coasted along the shore, ravaged the Locrian seaboard, and so returned home.

About this time the Lacedaemonians founded their colony of Heraclea in Trachis, with this object in view. The Malians form three tribes in all — the Paralians, the Hiereans, and the Trachinians. The Trachinians, having suffered severely in a war with their neighbours the Oetaeans, at first intended to put themselves under Athens; but afterwards, fearing they would not find with her the security they sought, they sent to Lacedaemon, having chosen Tisamenus as their ambassador. The Dorians, from the mother country of the Lacedaemonians, joined this embassy with the same request, since they too were suffering from the same enemy. After hearing them, the Lacedaemonians decided to send out the colony, both to help the Trachinians and Dorians and because they thought the proposed town would lie conveniently for the war against the Athenians. A fleet might be readied there against Euboea, with the advantage of a short crossing to the island; and the town would also be useful as a station on the road to Thrace. In short, everything made the Lacedaemonians eager to found the place. After first consulting the god at Delphi and getting a favourable answer, they sent off the colonists, Spartans and Perioeci, also inviting any of the rest of the Hellenes who wished to join, except Ionians, Achaeans, and certain other peoples. Three Lacedaemonians led as founders of the colony — Leon, Alcidas, and Damagon. With the settlement made, they freshly fortified the city, now called Heraclea, about four and a half miles from Thermopylae and two and a quarter from the sea, and began building docks, closing the side toward Thermopylae just at the pass itself, so that they could be easily defended.

The foundation of this town, evidently meant to harass Euboea (the crossing to Cenaeum on the island being a short one), at first caused some alarm at Athens, which the event, however, did nothing to justify, since the town never gave them any trouble. The reason was this. The Thessalians, who held sway in those parts and whose territory was threatened by its foundation, were afraid it might prove a powerful neighbour and so continually harassed and made war on the new settlers, until at last they wore them out, in spite of their originally considerable numbers — people had flocked from all quarters to a place founded by the Lacedaemonians and so thought sure of prosperity. On the other hand, the Lacedaemonians themselves, in the persons of their governors, did their full share towards ruining its prosperity and reducing its population, since they frightened away most of the inhabitants by governing harshly and in some cases unfairly, and so made it easier for their neighbours to prevail against them.

The same summer, around the time the Athenians were detained at Melos, their fellow citizens in the thirty ships cruising round the Peloponnese, after cutting off some guards in an ambush at Ellomenus in Leucadia, then went against Leucas itself with a large force, having been reinforced by the whole levy of the Acarnanians except Oeniadae, by the Zacynthians and Cephallenians, and by fifteen ships from Corcyra. While the Leucadians watched the devastation of their land, both outside and inside the isthmus on which the town of Leucas and the temple of Apollo stand, they made no move because of the overwhelming numbers of the enemy. The Acarnanians urged Demosthenes, the Athenian general, to build a wall to cut the town off from the mainland — a measure they were sure would secure its capture and rid them once and for all of a most troublesome enemy.

Demosthenes, however, had meanwhile been persuaded by the Messenians that this was a fine opportunity, with so large an army assembled, to attack the Aetolians, who were not only the enemies of Naupactus, but whose reduction would also make it easy to gain the rest of that part of the mainland for the Athenians. The Aetolian nation, although numerous and warlike, lived in unwalled villages scattered far apart and had nothing but light arms; according to the Messenians, they could be subdued without much difficulty before reinforcements could arrive. The plan they recommended was to attack first the Apodotians, then the Ophionians, and after them the Eurytanians, who are the largest tribe in Aetolia and speak, it is said, an extremely difficult language and eat their flesh raw. Once these were subdued, the rest would easily come in.

Demosthenes consented to this plan, both to please the Messenians and in the belief that, by adding the Aetolians to his other mainland allies, he would be able, without help from home, to march against the Boeotians by way of Ozolian Locris to Kytinium in Doris, keeping Parnassus on his right until he descended on the Phocians, whom he could compel to join him if their old friendship for Athens did not, as he expected, immediately decide them to do so. Once in Phocis he was already on the frontier of Boeotia. He accordingly weighed from Leucas, against the wish of the Acarnanians, and with his whole force sailed along the coast to Sollium, where he disclosed his plan to them. When they refused to agree, because of the failure to invest Leucas, he set out on his expedition against the Aetolians with the rest of the forces — the Cephallenians, the Messenians, the Zacynthians, and three hundred Athenian marines from his own ships (the fifteen Corcyraean ships had departed). He established his base at Oeneon in Locris, since the Ozolian Locrians were allies of Athens and were to meet him with all their forces in the interior. Being neighbours of the Aetolians and armed in the same way, they were thought likely to be of great service on the expedition, given their familiarity with the country and the way the inhabitants fought.

After bivouacking with the army in the precinct of Nemean Zeus, where the poet Hesiod is said to have been killed by the people of the country, in fulfilment of an oracle that had foretold he would die at Nemea, Demosthenes set out at daybreak to invade Aetolia. The first day he took Potidania, the next Krokyle, and the third Tichium, where he halted and sent the booty back to Eupalium in Locris, having decided to push his conquests as far as the Ophionians and, if they refused to submit, to return to Naupactus and make them the object of a second expedition. Meanwhile the Aetolians had been aware of his plan from the moment it was formed, and as soon as the army invaded their country they came up in great force with all their tribes — even the most remote Ophionians, the Bomiensians, and Calliensians, who extend toward the Malian Gulf, were among them.

The Messenians, however, stuck to their original advice. Assuring Demosthenes that the Aetolians were an easy conquest, they urged him to push on as fast as possible and to try to take the villages as fast as he came to them, not waiting until the whole nation was in arms against him. Led on by his advisers and trusting in his luck, since he had met no opposition, and without waiting for his Locrian reinforcements — who were to have supplied him with the light-armed darters in which he was most lacking — he advanced and stormed Aegitium. The inhabitants fled before him and posted themselves on the hills above the town, which stood on high ground about nine miles from the sea. Meanwhile the Aetolians had gathered to the rescue and now attacked the Athenians and their allies, running down from the hills on every side and hurling their javelins, falling back when the Athenian army advanced, and pressing on as it retired. For a long time the battle went on like this, advance and retreat in turn, with the Athenians getting the worse of both.

Still, as long as their archers had arrows left and could use them, they held out, the light-armed Aetolians retreating before the arrows; but after the captain of the archers had been killed and his men scattered, the soldiers, worn out by the constant repetition of the same exertions and hard pressed by the Aetolians with their javelins, at last turned and fled. Falling into trackless gullies and places they did not know, they perished there; their guide, the Messenian Chromon, having unfortunately also been killed. A great many were overtaken in the pursuit by the swift-footed light-armed Aetolians and fell beneath their javelins; but most missed their way and rushed into the wood, which had no exit, and which the enemy soon set on fire and burnt round them. The Athenian army fell victims to death in every form, and went through every hardship of flight; the survivors with difficulty escaped to the sea and to Oeneon in Locris, where they had set out from. Many of the allies were killed, and about one hundred and twenty Athenian heavy infantry — not a man less, all in the prime of life. These were by far the best men of the city of Athens to fall during this war. Among the slain was also Procles, the colleague of Demosthenes. The Athenians took up their dead under truce from the Aetolians and withdrew to Naupactus, and from there sailed in their ships to Athens; Demosthenes stayed behind in Naupactus and the surrounding area, afraid to face the Athenians after the disaster.
About the same time the Athenians on the coast of Sicily sailed to Locris, and in a landing they made from the ships defeated the Locrians who came against them and took a fort on the river Halex.

The same summer the Aetolians, who before the Athenian expedition had sent an embassy to Corinth and Lacedaemon — composed of Tolophus, an Ophionian, Boriades, an Eurytanian, and Tisander, an Apodotian — obtained an army to be sent to them against Naupactus, which had brought on the Athenian invasion. The Lacedaemonians accordingly sent off, towards autumn, three thousand allied heavy infantry, five hundred of whom were from Heraclea, the newly founded city in Trachis, under the command of Eurylochus, a Spartan, accompanied by Macarius and Menedaius, also Spartans.

After the army had assembled at Delphi, Eurylochus sent a herald to the Ozolian Locrians, since the road to Naupactus lay through their territory and he had also conceived the idea of detaching them from Athens. His chief supporters in Locris were the Amphissians, alarmed at the hostility of the Phocians. They were the first to give hostages themselves and persuaded the rest to do the same out of fear of the invading army — first their neighbours the Myonians, who held the most difficult of the passes, and after them the Ipnians, Messapians, Tritaeans, Chalaeans, Tolophonians, Hessians, and Oeanthians, all of whom joined the expedition. The Olpaeans contented themselves with giving hostages without joining the invasion, while the Hyaeans refused to do either, until the capture of Polis, one of their villages.

His preparations complete, Eurylochus lodged the hostages in Kytinium, in Doris, and advanced upon Naupactus through the country of the Locrians, taking on his way Oeneon and Eupalium, two of their towns that refused to join him. Once in Naupactian territory, and now joined by the Aetolians, the army laid waste the land and took the suburb of the town, which was unfortified, and after this Molycrium too, a Corinthian colony subject to Athens. Meanwhile the Athenian Demosthenes, who since the affair in Aetolia had remained near Naupactus, having had word of the army and fearing for the town, went and persuaded the Acarnanians, although not without difficulty because he had left Leucas, to relieve Naupactus. They accordingly sent with him on board his ships a thousand heavy infantry, who threw themselves into the place and saved it; otherwise the extent of its wall and the small number of its defenders had put it in the greatest danger. Meanwhile Eurylochus and his companions, finding that this force had got in and that storming the town was impossible, withdrew, not to the Peloponnese, but to the country once called Aeolis and now Calydon and Pleuron, and to the places in that area, and to Proschium in Aetolia. The Ambraciots had come and urged them to combine with them in attacking Amphilochian Argos and the rest of Amphilochia and Acarnania, claiming that the conquest of these countries would bring all the mainland into alliance with Lacedaemon. Eurylochus consented to this, and dismissing the Aetolians, now stayed quiet with his army in those parts, until the time should come for the Ambraciots to take the field and for him to join them before Argos.

Summer was now over. The following winter the Athenians in Sicily, with their Hellenic allies and those of the Sicel subjects or allies of Syracuse who had revolted from her and joined their army, marched against the Sicel town of Inessa, the acropolis of which was held by the Syracusans. After attacking it without being able to take it, they retired. In the retreat the allies, marching after the Athenians, were attacked by the Syracusans from the fort, and a large part of their army was routed with great slaughter. After this Laches and the Athenians from the ships made some landings in Locris and, defeating the Locrians who came against them with Proxenus, son of Capaton, on the river Caicinus, took some arms and departed.

The same winter the Athenians purified Delos, in compliance, it appears, with a certain oracle. It had been purified before by Pisistratus the tyrant — not the whole island, but as much of it as could be seen from the temple. Now, however, the whole was purified in the following way. All the sepulchres of those who had died on Delos were taken up, and for the future it was ordered that no one was to be allowed to die or give birth to a child on the island; they were to be carried over to Rhenea, which is so close to Delos that Polycrates, tyrant of Samos, having added Rhenea to his other island conquests during his period of naval supremacy, dedicated it to the Delian Apollo by binding it to Delos with a chain.

After the purification, the Athenians celebrated for the first time the quinquennial festival of the Delian games. There had once been, indeed, a great gathering of the Ionians and the neighbouring islanders at Delos, who used to come to the festival as the Ionians now do to that of Ephesus; athletic and poetical contests took place there, and the cities brought choirs of dancers. Nothing can be clearer on this point than the following lines of Homer, taken from a hymn to Apollo:

Phœbus, wherever thou strayest, far or near, Delos was still of all thy haunts most dear. Thither the robed Ionians take their way With wife and child to keep thy holiday, Invoke thy favour on each manly game, And dance and sing in honour of thy name.

That there was also a poetical contest in which the Ionians went to compete is shown by the following, taken from the same hymn. After praising the Delian dance of the women, he ends his song of praise with these lines, in which he also alludes to himself:

Well, may Apollo keep you all! and so, Sweethearts, good-bye — yet tell me not I go Out from your hearts; and if in after hours Some other wanderer in this world of ours Touch at your shores, and ask your maidens here Who sings the songs the sweetest to your ear, Think of me then, and answer with a smile, ‘A blind old man of Scio’s rocky isle.’

Homer thus attests that there was once a great assembly and festival at Delos. In later times, although the islanders and the Athenians continued to send the choirs of dancers with sacrifices, the contests and most of the ceremonies were abolished, probably through hardship, until the Athenians on this occasion celebrated the games with the novelty of horse-races.

The same winter the Ambraciots, as they had promised Eurylochus when they retained his army, marched out against Amphilochian Argos with three thousand heavy infantry, and invading Argive territory occupied Olpae, a stronghold on a hill near the sea, formerly fortified by the Acarnanians and used as the place of assizes for their nation, about two and three-quarters miles from the city of Argos on the seacoast. Meanwhile the Acarnanians went with part of their forces to relieve Argos, and with the rest encamped in Amphilochia at the place called Crenae, or the Wells, to watch for Eurylochus and his Peloponnesians and prevent them from passing through and joining up with the Ambraciots. They also sent for Demosthenes, the commander of the Aetolian expedition, to be their leader, and for the twenty Athenian ships cruising off the Peloponnese under the command of Aristotle, son of Timocrates, and Hierophon, son of Antimnestus. The Ambraciots at Olpae, on their part, sent a messenger to their own city begging them to come with their full levy to their aid, fearing that Eurylochus’s army might not be able to push through the Acarnanians, and that they themselves might be forced to fight alone, or be unable to retreat without danger if they wished to.

Meanwhile Eurylochus and his Peloponnesians, learning that the Ambraciots at Olpae had arrived, set out from Proschium in all haste to join them. Crossing the Achelous, they advanced through Acarnania, which they found deserted by its population, who had gone to relieve Argos. They kept on their right the city of the Stratians and its garrison, and on their left the rest of Acarnania. Crossing the territory of the Stratians, they advanced through Phytia, then, skirting Medeon, through Limnaea; after which they left Acarnania behind and entered friendly country — that of the Agraeans. From there they reached and crossed Mount Thymaus, which belongs to the Agraeans, and descended into Argive territory after nightfall, and passing between the city of Argos and the Acarnanian posts at Crenae, joined the Ambraciots at Olpae.

Joining up here at daybreak, they sat down at the place called Metropolis and made camp. Not long after, the Athenians in the twenty ships came into the Ambracian Gulf to support the Argives, with Demosthenes and two hundred Messenian heavy infantry and sixty Athenian archers. While the fleet off Olpae blockaded the hill from the sea, the Acarnanians and a few of the Amphilochians — most of whom were held back by force by the Ambraciots — had already arrived at Argos and were preparing to give battle to the enemy, having chosen Demosthenes to command the whole of the allied army together with their own generals. Demosthenes led them up close to Olpae and encamped, with a great ravine separating the two armies. For five days they stayed inactive; on the sixth, both sides drew up in order of battle. The Peloponnesian army was the larger and outflanked their opponents; and Demosthenes, fearing that his right might be surrounded, posted in ambush in a hollow road overgrown with bushes some four hundred heavy infantry and light troops, who were to rise up at the moment of the onset behind the projecting left wing of the enemy and take them in the rear. When both sides were ready they joined battle. Demosthenes was on the right wing with the Messenians and a few Athenians, while the rest of the line was made up of the various divisions of the Acarnanians and of the Amphilochian darters. The Peloponnesians and Ambraciots were drawn up mixed together, except for the Mantineans, who were massed on the left, though not reaching to the very end of the wing, where Eurylochus and his men confronted the Messenians and Demosthenes.

The Peloponnesians, now well engaged, were just on the point of turning their enemy’s right with their outflanking wing, when the Acarnanians from the ambush set on them from behind and broke them at the first attack, without their staying to resist; the panic into which they fell caused the flight of most of their army, terrified beyond measure at seeing the division of Eurylochus and their best troops cut to pieces. Most of the work was done by Demosthenes and his Messenians, who were posted in this part of the field. Meanwhile the Ambraciots — the best soldiers in those countries — and the troops on the right wing defeated the division facing them and pursued it as far as Argos. Returning from the pursuit, they found their main body defeated; and hard pressed by the Acarnanians, with difficulty made their way through to Olpae, suffering heavy loss along the way as they dashed on without discipline or order — except for the Mantineans, who kept their ranks better than any other unit in the army during the retreat.

The battle did not end until evening. The next day Menedaius, who on the death of Eurylochus and Macarius had succeeded to sole command, was at a loss after such a signal defeat as to how to stay and stand a siege, cut off as he was on land and by the Athenian fleet at sea, and equally how to retreat in safety. He opened a parley with Demosthenes and the Acarnanian generals for a truce and permission to withdraw, and at the same time for the recovery of the dead. The dead they gave back, and after setting up a trophy they took up their own as well, about three hundred in number. The retreat asked for they refused publicly to the army; but permission to depart at once was secretly granted to the Mantineans and to Menedaius and the other commanders and leading men of the Peloponnesians by Demosthenes and his Acarnanian colleagues, who wanted to strip the Ambraciots and the mercenary host of foreigners of their supporters and, above all, to discredit the Lacedaemonians and Peloponnesians with the Hellenes in those parts as traitors and self-seekers.

While the enemy was taking up his dead and hastily burying them as best he could, and those who had gained permission were secretly arranging their retreat, word was brought to Demosthenes and the Acarnanians that the Ambraciots from the city, in compliance with the first message from Olpae, were on the march with their whole levy through Amphilochia to join their countrymen at Olpae, knowing nothing of what had happened. Demosthenes prepared to march out against them with his army, and meanwhile sent on at once a strong division to seize the roads and occupy the strong positions. In the meantime the Mantineans and others included in the agreement went out under the pretence of gathering herbs and firewood and slipped off in twos and threes, picking on the way the things they had pretended to come out for, until they had gone some distance from Olpae, when they quickened their pace. The Ambraciots and others who had accompanied them in larger parties, seeing them going on, pushed on in their turn and started running to catch up. The Acarnanians at first thought all alike were going off without permission and started to chase the Peloponnesians; believing they were being betrayed, they even threw a javelin or two at some of their generals who tried to stop them and explained that leave had been granted. In the end, however, they let the Mantineans and Peloponnesians pass, and killed only the Ambraciots — though there was much dispute and difficulty in telling whether a man was an Ambraciot or a Peloponnesian. The number killed in this way was about two hundred; the rest escaped into the bordering territory of Agraea and found refuge with Salynthius, the friendly king of the Agraeans.

Meanwhile the Ambraciots from the city reached Idomene. Idomene consists of two lofty hills, the higher of which the troops sent on by Demosthenes succeeded in occupying after nightfall, unobserved by the Ambraciots, who had meanwhile climbed the lower one and bivouacked under it. After supper Demosthenes set out with the rest of the army, as soon as it was evening: he himself with half his force made for the pass, while the rest went by way of the Amphilochian hills. At dawn he fell on the Ambraciots while they were still in bed, ignorant of what had happened, and fully thinking these were their own countrymen — Demosthenes having deliberately put the Messenians at the front with orders to address them in the Doric dialect and so inspire confidence in the sentries, who could not see them clearly since it was still dark. In this way he routed their army as soon as he attacked, killing most of them where they lay; the rest broke away in flight over the hills. The roads, however, were already occupied; and while the Amphilochians knew their own country, the Ambraciots did not and could not tell which way to turn, and besides they had heavy armour against a light-armed enemy. So they fell into ravines and into the ambushes that had been set for them, and perished there. In their many efforts to escape, some even turned to the sea, which was not far off, and seeing the Athenian ships coasting along the shore just while the action was going on, swam off to them, thinking it better in their panic to perish, if perish they must, by the hands of the Athenians than at those of the barbarous and detested Amphilochians. Of the great Ambraciot force destroyed in this way, only a few reached the city in safety; while the Acarnanians, after stripping the dead and setting up a trophy, returned to Argos.

The next day a herald arrived from the Ambraciots who had fled from Olpae to the Agraeans, asking leave to take up the dead that had fallen after the first engagement, when they had left the camp with the Mantineans and their companions, without, like them, having had permission. At the sight of the arms of the Ambraciots from the city, the herald was astonished at their number, knowing nothing of the disaster and imagining they belonged to his own party. Someone asked him what he was so astonished at, and how many of them had been killed — imagining, in his turn, that this was the herald from the troops at Idomene. He answered, “About two hundred”; at which his questioner cut him off, saying, “Why, the arms you see here are of more than a thousand.” The herald replied, “Then they are not the arms of those who fought with us?” The other answered, “Yes they are, if at least you fought at Idomene yesterday.” “But we fought no one yesterday; the day before, in the retreat.” “However that may be, we fought yesterday with those who came to reinforce you from the city of the Ambraciots.” When the herald heard this and realized that the reinforcement from the city had been wiped out, he broke into wailing and, stunned at the magnitude of the present evils, went away at once without performing his errand or asking again for the dead bodies. This was by far the greatest disaster that befell any single Hellenic city in the same number of days during this war; and I have not set down the number of the dead, since the figure given seems out of proportion to the size of the city, to the point of being incredible. In any case I know that, had the Acarnanians and Amphilochians wished to take Ambracia as the Athenians and Demosthenes advised, they could have done so without a blow; as it was, they feared that if the Athenians had it, they would be worse neighbours to them than the present ones.

After this the Acarnanians allotted a third of the spoils to the Athenians and divided the rest among their own different towns. The Athenians’ share was captured on the voyage home; the arms now deposited in the Attic temples are the three hundred panoplies which the Acarnanians set apart for Demosthenes, and which he brought to Athens in person — his return home after the Aetolian disaster being made less hazardous by this exploit. The Athenians in the twenty ships also went off to Naupactus. The Acarnanians and Amphilochians, after Demosthenes and the Athenians had departed, granted the Ambraciots and Peloponnesians who had taken refuge with Salynthius and the Agraeans a free withdrawal from Oeniadae, to which they had moved from Salynthius’ country, and for the future concluded a treaty and alliance with the Ambraciots for one hundred years on the following terms. It was to be a defensive alliance, not an offensive one: the Ambraciots could not be required to march with the Acarnanians against the Peloponnesians, nor the Acarnanians with the Ambraciots against the Athenians; for the rest, the Ambraciots were to give up the places and hostages they held of the Amphilochians, and not to give help to Anactorium, which was at odds with the Acarnanians. With this arrangement they put an end to the war. After this the Corinthians sent a garrison of their own citizens to Ambracia — three hundred heavy infantry under the command of Xenocleides, son of Euthycles, who reached their destination after a difficult journey overland. Such was the history of the Ambracia affair.

The same winter the Athenians in Sicily made a landing from their ships in the territory of Himera, in concert with the Sicels, who had invaded its borders from the interior, and also sailed to the islands of Aeolus. On their return to Rhegium they found the Athenian general Pythodorus, son of Isolochus, had come to relieve Laches in command of the fleet. The allies in Sicily had sailed to Athens and induced the Athenians to send out more ships to their aid, pointing out that the Syracusans, who already had control of the land, were making efforts to put together a navy, to avoid being any longer kept off the sea by a few ships. The Athenians proceeded to man forty ships to send them, thinking the war in Sicily would thus be ended sooner, and also wanting to give their navy practice. One of the generals, Pythodorus, was accordingly sent out with a few ships; Sophocles, son of Sostratides, and Eurymedon, son of Thucles, were to follow with the main body. Meanwhile Pythodorus had taken command of Laches’ ships, and toward the end of winter sailed against the Locrian fort that Laches had previously taken, and returned after being defeated in battle by the Locrians.

In the first days of the spring, the stream of fire issued from Etna, as on previous occasions, and destroyed some of the land of the Catanians, who live on Mount Etna, the largest mountain in Sicily. Fifty years, it is said, had passed since the previous eruption — there having been three in all since the Hellenes have inhabited Sicily. Such were the events of this winter; and with it ended the sixth year of this war of which Thucydides was the historian.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 12 — Seventh Year of the War—Occupation of Pylos—Surrender of the Spartan Army in Sphacteria
paragraphs: Next summer, about the time the corn was coming into ear, ten Syracusan and as many Locrian vessels sailed to Messina, in Sicily, and occupied the town at the invitation of the inhabitants; and Messina revolted from the Athenians. The Syracusans contrived this chiefly because they saw the place gave them an approach to Sicily and feared that the Athenians might later use it as a base for attacking them with a larger force. The Locrians did so because they wished to carry on hostilities from both sides of the strait and reduce their enemies, the people of Rhegium. Meanwhile the Locrians had invaded Rhegian territory with all their forces, to prevent them helping Messina, and also at the urging of some Rhegian exiles who were with them; the long factional struggles by which Rhegium had been torn made it for the moment incapable of resistance, and so provided an additional temptation for the invaders. After devastating the country the Locrian land forces withdrew, their ships remaining to guard Messina, while others were being manned for the same destination to carry on the war from there.

About the same time in the spring, before the corn was ripe, the Peloponnesians and their allies invaded Attica under Agis, son of Archidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians, and sat down and laid waste the country. Meanwhile the Athenians sent off the forty ships they had been preparing for Sicily, with the remaining generals Eurymedon and Sophocles; their colleague Pythodorus had already gone ahead. These had also been instructed to look in, as they sailed by, on the Corcyraeans in the town, who were being plundered by the exiles in the mountains. To support these exiles, sixty Peloponnesian vessels had recently sailed there, since it was thought that the famine raging in the city would make it easy for them to reduce it. Demosthenes too, who had remained without employment since his return from Acarnania, applied for and obtained permission to use the fleet, if he wished, on the coast of the Peloponnese.

Off Laconia they heard that the Peloponnesian ships were already at Corcyra, and Eurymedon and Sophocles wished to hurry to the island. But Demosthenes asked them first to touch at Pylos and do what was needed there before continuing the voyage. While they were objecting, a squall came on and carried the fleet into Pylos. Demosthenes at once urged them to fortify the place—it was for this that he had come on the voyage—and pointed out that there was plenty of stone and timber on the spot, that the place was strong by nature, and that, together with much of the country round, it was unoccupied. Pylos, or Coryphasium, as the Lacedaemonians call it, is about forty-five miles from Sparta, and lies in the old country of the Messenians. The commanders told him that there was no shortage of deserted headlands in the Peloponnese if he wanted to put the city to expense by occupying them. He thought, however, that this place was distinguished from others of its kind by having a harbour close by, and that the Messenians, the old natives of the country, who spoke the same dialect as the Lacedaemonians, could do them the greatest harm by raids from it, and would at the same time make a trustworthy garrison.

After speaking to the captains of companies on the subject and failing to persuade either the generals or the soldiers, he stayed inactive with the rest because of the weather; until the soldiers themselves, wanting something to do, were seized with a sudden impulse to go round and fortify the place. They set to work in earnest. Having no iron tools, they picked up stones and put them together as they happened to fit; and where mortar was needed, they carried it on their backs for want of hods, stooping down to keep it on, and clasping their hands together behind to prevent it falling off. They spared no effort to be able to complete the most vulnerable points before the Lacedaemonians arrived, since most of the place was sufficiently strong by nature to need no further fortification.

Meanwhile the Lacedaemonians were celebrating a festival, and at first they made light of the news, thinking that whenever they chose to take the field the place would be immediately abandoned by the enemy or easily taken by force; the absence of their army before Athens also had something to do with their delay. The Athenians fortified the place on the land side, and where it most required it, in six days, and leaving Demosthenes with five ships to garrison it, hurried on with the main body of the fleet on their voyage to Corcyra and Sicily.

As soon as the Peloponnesians in Attica heard of the occupation of Pylos, they hurried back home; the Lacedaemonians and their king Agis felt that the matter touched them closely. Besides having made their invasion early in the season, while the corn was still green, most of their troops were short of provisions; the weather too was unusually bad for the time of year, and greatly distressed their army. Many reasons combined to hasten their departure and make this invasion a very short one—indeed they only stayed fifteen days in Attica.

About the same time the Athenian general Simonides, gathering a few Athenians from the garrisons and a number of allies in those parts, took Eion in Thrace, a Mendaean colony hostile to Athens, by treachery. But no sooner had he done so than the Chalcidians and Bottiaeans came up and beat him out of it, with the loss of many of his soldiers.

On the return of the Peloponnesians from Attica, the Spartans themselves and the nearest of the Perioeci at once set out for Pylos, the other Lacedaemonians following more slowly, since they had just come in from another campaign. Word was also sent round the Peloponnese to come up as quickly as possible to Pylos. The sixty Peloponnesian ships were summoned from Corcyra, and being dragged by their crews across the isthmus of Leucas, passed unnoticed by the Athenian squadron at Zacynthus and reached Pylos, where the land forces had arrived before them. Before the Peloponnesian fleet sailed in, Demosthenes found time to send out, unobserved, two ships to inform Eurymedon and the Athenians on board the fleet at Zacynthus of the danger to Pylos and to summon them to his assistance. While the ships hastened on their voyage in obedience to Demosthenes’ orders, the Lacedaemonians prepared to assault the fort by land and sea, hoping easily to capture a work built in haste and held by a feeble garrison. Meanwhile, expecting the Athenian ships to arrive from Zacynthus, they intended, if they failed to take the place first, to block the entrances to the harbour to keep them from anchoring inside it. The island of Sphacteria, stretching in a line close in front of the harbour, both makes the harbour safe and narrows its entrances, leaving a passage for two ships on the side nearest Pylos and the Athenian fortifications, and for eight or nine on the side nearest the rest of the mainland. The rest of the island was entirely covered with wood and trackless, since uninhabited, and about one mile and five furlongs in length. The Lacedaemonians meant to close the inlets with a line of ships placed close together, prows turned toward the sea. Meanwhile, fearing that the enemy might use the island as a base against them, they carried over some heavy infantry to it, stationing others along the coast. By this means the island and the mainland would both be hostile to the Athenians, who would not be able to land on either; and the shore of Pylos itself, outside the inlet toward the open sea, having no harbour, offered no point that could be used as a base to relieve their countrymen. Without a sea-fight or risk, the Lacedaemonians would in all likelihood become masters of a place taken on the spur of the moment and unprovided with provisions. With this decided, they carried over to the island the heavy infantry, drafted by lot from all the companies. Some others had crossed earlier in relief parties, but those who were left there in this final draft numbered four hundred and twenty, with their Helot attendants, commanded by Epitadas, son of Molobrus.

Meanwhile Demosthenes, seeing that the Lacedaemonians were about to attack him by sea and land at once, was not idle. He drew up under the fortification, and enclosed in a stockade, the galleys remaining to him from those left him, arming the sailors taken out of them with poor shields, most of them made of osier; for it was impossible to procure arms in such a deserted place, and even these had been obtained from a thirty-oared Messenian privateer and a boat belonging to some Messenians who happened to have come there. Among these Messenians were forty heavy infantry, whom he made use of with the rest. He posted most of his men, armed and unarmed, on the best-fortified and strongest points of the place toward the interior, with orders to repel any attack of the land forces. He picked sixty heavy infantry and a few archers from his whole force, and with these went outside the wall down to the sea, where he thought the enemy would most likely try to land. The ground was difficult and rocky, looking out toward the open sea; but the very fact that this was the weakest part of the wall would, he thought, encourage their eagerness, since the Athenians, confident in their naval superiority, had paid little attention to the defences here, and the enemy, if he could force a landing, might feel sure of taking the place. At this point, accordingly, going down to the water’s edge, he posted his heavy infantry to prevent a landing if possible, and encouraged them with these words:

“Soldiers and comrades in this adventure, I hope none of you in our present strait will think to show his wit by exactly calculating all the perils that surround us. I hope rather that you will hasten to close with the enemy without staying to count the odds, seeing in this our best chance of safety. In emergencies like ours, calculation is out of place; the sooner the danger is faced, the better. To my mind, too, most of the chances are for us, if we will only stand fast and not throw away our advantages, overawed by the enemy’s numbers. One point in our favour is the awkwardness of the landing. This, however, only helps us if we stand our ground. If we give way it will be practicable enough, in spite of its natural difficulty, with no defender; and the enemy will at once become more formidable, since retreat will be hard for him if we manage to repulse him—which we shall find easier to do while he is on board his ships than after he has landed and meets us on equal terms. As to his numbers, do not be too alarmed. Large as they are, he can only engage in small detachments, since it is impossible for many to put in to shore at once. Besides, the numerical superiority we have to face is not that of an army on land with everything else equal, but of troops on board ship, where many favourable accidents are needed to bring numbers to bear. I therefore consider that his difficulties may fairly be set against our numerical inferiority. At the same time, I charge you, as Athenians who know by experience what landing from ships on hostile territory means, and how impossible it is to drive back an enemy determined enough to stand his ground and not to be frightened off by the surf or the terrors of incoming ships, to stand fast in this present emergency, beat the enemy back at the water’s edge, and save yourselves and the place.”

Thus encouraged by Demosthenes, the Athenians felt more confident, and went down to meet the enemy, posting themselves along the edge of the sea. The Lacedaemonians now moved forward and at the same time assaulted the fortification with their land forces and their ships—forty-three in number—under their admiral, Thrasymelidas, son of Cratesicles, a Spartan, who made his attack just where Demosthenes expected. The Athenians thus had to defend themselves on both sides, from land and from sea. The enemy rowed up in small detachments, one relieving the other—it being impossible for many to put in at once—showing great ardour and cheering each other on, in the effort to force a passage and take the fortification. The man who most distinguished himself was Brasidas. Captain of a galley, and seeing that the captains and steersmen, struck by the difficulty of the position, hung back even where a landing seemed possible, for fear of wrecking their vessels, he shouted to them that they must never allow the enemy to fortify himself in their country for the sake of saving timber, but must shatter their ships and force a landing. He told the allies, instead of hesitating at such a moment to sacrifice their ships for Lacedaemon in return for her many benefits, to run them boldly aground, land in one way or another, and make themselves masters of the place and its garrison.

Not content with this exhortation, he forced his own steersman to run his ship ashore, and stepping onto the gangway was attempting to land when he was cut down by the Athenians, and after receiving many wounds fainted away. Falling into the bows, his shield slipped off his arm into the sea, was washed ashore, and was picked up by the Athenians, who afterwards used it for the trophy they set up for this attack. The rest also did their best, but were unable to land, owing to the difficulty of the ground and the unflinching tenacity of the Athenians. It was a strange reversal of the order of things for Athenians to be fighting from the land—and from Laconian land too—against Lacedaemonians coming from the sea, while the Lacedaemonians were trying to land from shipboard in their own country, now turned hostile, in order to attack Athenians; though the former were chiefly famous at the time as an inland people superior on land, and the latter as a maritime people with a navy that had no equal.

After continuing their attacks during that day and most of the next, the Peloponnesians desisted, and the day after sent some of their ships to Asine for timber to make engines, hoping with their help to take, in spite of its height, the wall opposite the harbour, where the landing was easiest. At this moment the Athenian fleet from Zacynthus arrived, now numbering fifty sail, having been reinforced by some of the ships on guard at Naupactus and by four Chian vessels. Seeing the coast and the island both crowded with heavy infantry, and the hostile ships in harbour showing no signs of sailing out, at a loss where to anchor, they sailed for the moment to the deserted island of Prote, not far off, where they spent the night. The next day they got under way, ready to engage in the open sea if the enemy chose to come out and meet them, and determined, if he did not, to sail in and attack him. The Lacedaemonians did not put out, and having failed to close the inlets as they had intended, remained quiet on shore, busy manning their ships and getting ready, in case anyone sailed in, to fight inside the harbour, which is fairly large.

Seeing this, the Athenians advanced against them by each inlet, and falling on the enemy’s fleet, most of which by this time was afloat and in line, at once put it to flight. Giving chase as far as the short distance allowed, they disabled a good many vessels and took five, one with its crew on board. They dashed in at the rest that had taken refuge on shore, battered some that were still being manned before they could put out, lashed others to their own ships and towed them off empty after the crews had fled. At this sight the Lacedaemonians, maddened by a disaster which cut off their men on the island, rushed to the rescue, going into the sea in their heavy armour, laying hold of the ships and trying to drag them back, every man thinking that success depended on his own exertions. Great was the melee, and quite contrary to the naval tactics usual to the two combatants: the Lacedaemonians in their excitement and dismay were actually engaged in a sea-fight on land, while the victorious Athenians, eager to push their success as far as possible, were carrying on a land-fight from their ships. After great exertions and many wounds on both sides, they separated, the Lacedaemonians saving their empty ships, except those first taken; and both parties returning to their camp, the Athenians set up a trophy, gave back the dead, secured the wrecks, and at once began to cruise round and watch the island jealously, with its trapped garrison; while the Peloponnesians on the mainland, whose contingents had now all come up, stayed where they were before Pylos.

When the news of what had happened at Pylos reached Sparta, the disaster was thought so serious that the Lacedaemonians resolved that the authorities should go down to the camp and decide on the spot what was best to be done. There, seeing it was impossible to help their men, and not wishing to risk their being reduced by hunger or overpowered by numbers, they determined, with the consent of the Athenian generals, to conclude an armistice at Pylos and send envoys to Athens to obtain a settlement and try to recover their men as quickly as possible.
The generals accepted their offers, and an armistice was concluded on the following terms:

That the Lacedaemonians should bring to Pylos and hand over to the Athenians the ships that had fought in the recent engagement, and all the warships in Laconia, and should make no attack on the fortification either by land or by sea.

That the Athenians should allow the Lacedaemonians on the mainland to send to the men on the island a fixed quantity of corn ready kneaded—two quarts of barley meal, one pint of wine, and a piece of meat for each man, and half the same quantity for a servant.
That this allowance should be sent in under the eyes of the Athenians, and that no boat should sail to the island except openly.
That the Athenians should continue to watch the island as before, but not land on it, and should refrain from attacking the Peloponnesian troops either by land or by sea.
That if either party should infringe any of these terms in the slightest particular, the armistice should at once be void.

That the armistice should hold until the return of the Lacedaemonian envoys from Athens—the Athenians sending them there in a galley and bringing them back—and on the arrival of the envoys should end, and the ships be restored by the Athenians in the same state as they received them.
Such were the terms of the armistice, and the ships were handed over to the number of sixty, and the envoys sent off accordingly. On reaching Athens they spoke as follows:

“Athenians, the Lacedaemonians have sent us to try to find some way of settling the affair of our men on the island, in a manner at once satisfactory to our interests and as consistent with our dignity in misfortune as circumstances permit. We can venture to speak at some length, without departing from the habit of our country. Men of few words where many are not wanted, we can be less brief when there is a matter of importance to be illustrated, and an end to be served by its illustration. Meanwhile we beg you to take what we say not in a hostile spirit, nor as if we thought you ignorant and wished to lecture you, but rather as a suggestion on the best course to be taken, addressed to intelligent judges. You can now, if you choose, employ your present success to advantage—keep what you have got and gain honour and reputation besides—and you can avoid the mistake of those who meet with an extraordinary piece of good fortune and are led on by hope to grasp continually at something further, having already succeeded beyond their expectations. Those who have known the most ups and downs of fortune are also rightly the least disposed to trust their prosperity; and to teach your city and ours this lesson, experience has not been wanting.

“To be convinced of this, you have only to look at our present misfortune. What power in Hellas stood higher than ours? Yet here we are coming to you, although we used to think ourselves more able to grant what we are now here to ask. Nevertheless, we have not been brought to this by any decay in our power, or by having had our heads turned by aggrandisement; our resources are what they have always been, and our error has been an error of judgment, to which all are equally liable. The prosperity that your city now enjoys, and the additions it has lately received, must not therefore make you fancy that fortune will always be with you. Sensible men are prudent enough to treat their gains as precarious, just as they would also keep a clear head in adversity, and they think that war, far from staying within the limits a combatant may wish to confine it to, will run the course its chances prescribe. Thus, not being puffed up by confidence in military success, they are less likely to come to grief, and most ready to make peace, if they can, while their fortune lasts. This, Athenians, is a good opportunity for you to do now with us, and so to escape the possible disasters that may follow from refusal—and the consequent imputation of having owed even your present advantages to accident, when you might have left behind you a reputation for power and wisdom that nothing could endanger.

“The Lacedaemonians accordingly invite you to make a treaty and to end the war, and offer peace, alliance, and the most friendly and intimate relations in every way and on every occasion between us; and in return ask for the men on the island, thinking it better for both parties not to hold out to the end—on the chance of some favourable accident enabling the men to force their way out, or of their being compelled to succumb under the pressure of blockade. Indeed, if great enmities are ever to be really settled, we think it will not be by the system of revenge and military success, by forcing an opponent to swear to a treaty to his disadvantage; but when the more fortunate combatant waives these privileges, lets gentler feelings guide him, conquers his rival in generosity, and grants peace on more moderate conditions than expected. From that moment, instead of the debt of revenge that violence must entail, his adversary owes a debt of generosity to be repaid in kind, and is inclined by honour to stand by his agreement. Men more often act in this way toward their greatest enemies than where the quarrel is of less importance; they are also by nature as glad to give way to those who first yield to them as they are quick to be provoked by arrogance into risks their own judgment condemns.

“To apply this to ourselves: if peace was ever desirable for both parties, it is surely so at the present moment—before anything irremediable happens to us and forces us to hate you eternally, personally as well as politically, and you to miss the advantages we now offer you.
