While the issue is still in doubt, and you have reputation and our friendship in prospect, and we the compromise of our misfortune before anything fatal has occurred, let us be reconciled. Choose peace instead of war for ourselves, and grant the rest of the Hellenes a remission from their sufferings, for which, you may be sure, they will think they have chiefly you to thank. The war that they are suffering through, they do not know which side started; but the peace that ends it, since it depends on your decision, will be laid to your door by their gratitude. By such a decision you can become firm friends with the Lacedaemonians at their own invitation—not forced from them, but obliged by your acceptance. Consider too the advantages likely to follow from this friendship: when Attica and Sparta are at one, the rest of Hellas, you may be sure, will remain in respectful inferiority before its leaders.”

Such were the words of the Lacedaemonians. Their idea was that the Athenians, already wanting a truce and held back only by their opposition, would joyfully accept a peace freely offered and give back the men. The Athenians, however, having the men on the island, thought that the treaty would be ready for them whenever they chose to make it, and grasped at something further. Foremost in encouraging them in this policy was Cleon, son of Cleaenetus, a popular leader of the time, very powerful with the multitude, who persuaded them to answer as follows. First, the men on the island must surrender themselves and their arms and be brought to Athens. Next, the Lacedaemonians must restore Nisaea, Pegae, Troezen, and Achaia—all places acquired not by arms but by the previous convention, under which they had been ceded by Athens herself at a moment of disaster, when a truce was more necessary to her than at present. This done, they could take their men back and make a truce for as long as both parties might agree.

To this answer the envoys made no reply, but asked that commissioners be chosen with whom they might confer on each point, quietly talking the matter over and trying to come to some agreement. At this Cleon violently attacked them, saying he had known from the first they had no honest intentions, and that this was now plain enough from their refusing to speak before the people and wanting instead to confer in secret with a committee of two or three. If they meant anything honest, let them say it out before all. The Lacedaemonians, however, seeing that whatever concessions they might be prepared to make in their misfortune, it was impossible to speak before the multitude and lose credit with their allies for a negotiation that might in the end miscarry, and on the other hand that the Athenians would never grant what they asked on moderate terms, returned from Athens having achieved nothing.

Their arrival at once put an end to the armistice at Pylos, and the Lacedaemonians asked back their ships under the convention. The Athenians, however, alleged an attack on the fort in violation of the truce, along with other grievances seemingly not worth mentioning, and refused to give them back, insisting on the clause by which the slightest infringement made the armistice void. The Lacedaemonians, after denying the violation and protesting against bad faith in the matter of the ships, went away and earnestly addressed themselves to the war. Hostilities were now carried on at Pylos with vigour on both sides. The Athenians cruised round the island all day with two ships going opposite ways, and at night anchored round it with their whole fleet, except on the seaward side in windy weather. The fleet had been reinforced by twenty ships from Athens come to aid in the blockade, and now numbered seventy sail. The Peloponnesians remained encamped on the continent, making attacks on the fort and watching for any opportunity that might offer for the deliverance of their men.

Meanwhile the Syracusans and their allies in Sicily had brought up to the squadron guarding Messina the reinforcement we left them preparing, and were carrying on the war from there, incited chiefly by the Locrians out of hatred for the Rhegians, whose territory they had invaded with all their forces. The Syracusans also wished to try their fortune at sea, seeing that the Athenians had only a few ships actually at Rhegium, and hearing that the main fleet meant to join them was engaged in blockading the island. A naval victory, they thought, would let them blockade Rhegium by sea and land and easily reduce it; a success that would at once place their affairs on a solid footing, since the promontory of Rhegium in Italy and Messina in Sicily are so near each other that it would be impossible for the Athenians to cruise against them and command the strait. The strait in question consists of the sea between Rhegium and Messina, at the point where Sicily comes nearest to the continent, and is the Charybdis through which the story makes Ulysses sail. The narrowness of the passage and the strength of the current that pours in from the vast Tyrrhenian and Sicilian mains have rightly given it a bad reputation.

In this strait the Syracusans and their allies were forced to fight, late in the day, over the passage of a boat, putting out with rather more than thirty ships against sixteen Athenian and eight Rhegian vessels. Defeated by the Athenians, they hurried off, each man for himself, to their own stations at Messina and Rhegium, with the loss of one ship; night came on before the battle was finished. After this the Locrians retired from Rhegian territory, and the ships of the Syracusans and their allies united and came to anchor at Cape Pelorus, in Messinian territory, where their land forces joined them. Here the Athenians and Rhegians sailed up, and seeing the ships unmanned, made an attack, in which they in turn lost one vessel, caught by a grappling iron, the crew saving themselves by swimming. After this the Syracusans got on board their ships, and while they were being towed alongshore to Messina were attacked again by the Athenians, but suddenly got out to sea and became the assailants, causing them to lose another vessel. After thus holding their own in the voyage alongshore and in the engagement just described, the Syracusans sailed on into the harbour of Messina.

Meanwhile the Athenians, having received warning that Camarina was about to be betrayed to the Syracusans by Archias and his party, sailed there. The Messinese took this opportunity to attack their Chalcidian neighbour, Naxos, by sea and land with all their forces. The first day they forced the Naxians to keep within their walls, and laid waste their country; the next they sailed round with their ships and laid waste their land along the river Akesines, while their land forces threatened the city. Meanwhile the Sicels came down from the high country in great numbers, to aid against the Messinese; and the Naxians, elated at the sight, and animated by a belief that the Leontines and their other Hellenic allies were coming to support them, suddenly sallied out from the town, attacked, and routed the Messinese, killing more than a thousand of them. The remainder suffered severely on their retreat home, attacked by the barbarians on the road, and most of them were cut off. The ships put in at Messina, and afterwards dispersed for their various homes. The Leontines and their allies, with the Athenians, at once turned their arms against the now weakened Messina, and attacked—the Athenians with their ships on the side of the harbour, the land forces on the side of the town. The Messinese, however, sallying out with Demoteles and some Locrians who had been left to garrison the city after the disaster, suddenly attacked and routed most of the Leontine army, killing a great number. On seeing this the Athenians landed from their ships, and falling on the Messinese in disorder chased them back into the town, and after setting up a trophy retired to Rhegium. After this the Hellenes in Sicily continued to make war on each other by land, without the Athenians.

Meanwhile the Athenians at Pylos were still besieging the Lacedaemonians on the island, the Peloponnesian forces on the mainland remaining where they were. The blockade was very laborious for the Athenians from want of food and water; there was no spring except one in the citadel of Pylos itself, and that not a large one, and most of them were forced to grub up the shingle on the sea beach and drink such water as they could find. They also suffered from lack of room, being encamped in a narrow space; and as there was no anchorage for the ships, some took their meals on shore in turn while the others were anchored out at sea. But their greatest discouragement came from the unexpectedly long time it was taking to reduce a body of men shut up on a deserted island, with only brackish water to drink—a matter they had imagined would take only a few days. The fact was that the Lacedaemonians had advertised for volunteers to carry into the island ground corn, wine, cheese, and any other food useful in a siege; high prices were offered, and freedom promised to any of the Helots who succeeded in doing so. The Helots accordingly were most forward to engage in this risky traffic, putting off from this or that part of the Peloponnese and running in by night on the seaward side of the island. They were best pleased, however, when they could catch a wind to carry them in. It was easier to evade the patrol of galleys when it blew from the seaward, since it became impossible for them to anchor round the island; and the Helots, having had their boats valued in money, ran them ashore without caring how they landed, sure of finding the soldiers waiting at the landing places. But all who risked it in fair weather were taken. Divers also swam in under water from the harbour, dragging by a cord in skins poppyseed mixed with honey, and bruised linseed; these at first escaped notice, but afterwards a watch was kept for them. In short, both sides tried every possible contrivance, the one to throw in provisions, the other to prevent their introduction.

At Athens, meanwhile, the news that the army was in great distress, and that corn was finding its way in to the men on the island, caused no small perplexity. The Athenians began to fear that winter might come on and find them still engaged in the blockade. They saw that convoying provisions round the Peloponnese would then be impossible. The country offered no resources in itself, and even in summer they could not send round enough. The blockade of a place without harbours could no longer be kept up; and the men would either escape, by the siege being abandoned, or watch for bad weather and sail out in the boats that brought their corn. What caused still more alarm was the attitude of the Lacedaemonians, who, the Athenians thought, must feel themselves on strong ground not to send any more envoys; and they began to repent having rejected the treaty. Cleon, perceiving the disfavour with which he was regarded for having stood in the way of the convention, now said that the informants did not speak the truth; and when the messengers recommended that, if they did not believe them, some commissioners be sent to see, Cleon himself and Theagenes were chosen by the Athenians as commissioners. Aware that he would now be obliged either to say what had already been said by the men he was slandering, or be proved a liar if he said the contrary, he told the Athenians—whom he saw were not entirely disinclined for a fresh expedition—that, instead of sending and wasting their time and opportunities, if they believed what they were told, they ought to sail against the men. And pointing at Nicias, son of Niceratus, then general, whom he hated, he tauntingly said that it would be easy, if they had men for generals, to sail with a force and take those on the island; and if he himself had been in command, he would have done it.

Nicias, seeing the Athenians murmuring against Cleon for not sailing now if it seemed to him so easy, and further seeing himself the object of attack, told him that for all the generals cared he might take what force he chose and make the attempt. At first Cleon thought this resignation was merely a figure of speech, and was ready to go; but finding it was meant seriously he drew back, and said that Nicias, not he, was general, being now frightened, and never having supposed that Nicias would go so far as to retire in his favour. Nicias, however, repeated his offer, resigned the command against Pylos, and called the Athenians to witness that he did so. And as the multitude is wont to do, the more Cleon shrank from the expedition and tried to back out of what he had said, the more they encouraged Nicias to hand over his command, and clamoured for Cleon to go. At last, not knowing how to escape his words, he undertook the expedition, came forward, and said that he was not afraid of the Lacedaemonians, but would sail without taking anyone from the city with him, except the Lemnians and Imbrians who were at Athens, with some targeteers who had come up from Aenus, and four hundred archers from other quarters. With these and the soldiers at Pylos, he would within twenty days either bring the Lacedaemonians back alive or kill them on the spot. The Athenians could not help laughing at his fatuity, while sensible men comforted themselves with the reflection that they were bound to gain in either case: either they would be rid of Cleon, which they rather hoped, or, if disappointed in this hope, they would reduce the Lacedaemonians.

After he had settled everything in the assembly, and the Athenians had voted him the command of the expedition, he chose as his colleague Demosthenes, one of the generals at Pylos, and pushed forward preparations for the voyage. His choice fell on Demosthenes because he heard that he was contemplating a descent on the island. The soldiers, distressed by the difficulties of the position, and rather besieged than besiegers, were eager to fight it out, while the firing of the island had increased their general’s confidence. He had been afraid at first because the island, never having been inhabited, was almost entirely covered with wood and trackless, thinking this in the enemy’s favour: he might land with a large force and yet suffer loss from an attack from an unseen position. The enemy’s mistakes and the strength of his forces would be largely concealed from him by the wood, while every blunder of his own troops would be at once detected, so that they could fall on him unexpectedly just where they pleased, the attack being always in their power. If, on the other hand, he forced them to engage in the thicket, the smaller number who knew the country would, he thought, have the advantage over the larger who did not, while his own army might be cut off imperceptibly, despite its numbers, since the men would not be able to see where to help one another.

The Aetolian disaster, which had been mainly caused by the wood, had no small part in these reflections. Meanwhile, one of the soldiers who were forced by want of room to land on the extremities of the island and take their dinners, with outposts set to prevent surprise, set fire to a little of the wood without meaning to; and as it came on to blow soon afterwards, almost the whole was consumed before they realised what had happened. Demosthenes was now able for the first time to see how numerous the Lacedaemonians really were—up to that moment he had been under the impression that they took in provisions for a smaller number. He also saw that the Athenians thought success important and were anxious about it, and that it was now easier to land on the island. Accordingly he got ready for the attempt, sent for troops from the allies in the neighbourhood, and pushed forward his other preparations. At this moment Cleon arrived at Pylos with the troops he had asked for, having sent word ahead that he was coming. The first step taken by the two generals after meeting was to send a herald to the camp on the mainland, to ask if they were disposed to avoid all risk and order the men on the island to surrender themselves and their arms, to be kept in mild custody until some general convention should be concluded.

On the rejection of this proposal, the generals let one day pass; the next, embarking all their heavy infantry on a few ships, they put out by night, and a little before dawn landed on both sides of the island from the open sea and from the harbour, about eight hundred strong, and advanced at a run against the first post on the island.

The enemy had distributed his force as follows. At this first post there were about thirty heavy infantry; the centre and most level part, where the water was, was held by the main body and by Epitadas their commander; while a small party guarded the very end of the island, toward Pylos, which was sheer on the seaward side and very hard to attack from the land, and where there was also a sort of old fort of stones rudely put together, which they thought might be useful to them if they were forced to retreat. Such was their disposition.

The advanced post thus attacked by the Athenians was at once put to the sword, the men being scarcely out of bed and still arming, the landing having taken them by surprise, since they thought the ships were only sailing as usual to their stations for the night. As soon as day broke, the rest of the army landed—that is, all the crews of rather more than seventy ships, except the lowest rank of oars, with the arms they carried, eight hundred archers, and as many targeteers, the Messenian reinforcements, and all the other troops on duty round Pylos, except the garrison on the fort. Demosthenes’ tactics had divided them into companies of two hundred, more or less, and sent them to occupy the highest points, in order to paralyse the enemy by surrounding him on every side and so leaving him without any tangible adversary, exposed to the cross-fire of their host. He would be plied by those in his rear if he attacked in front, and by those on one flank if he moved against those on the other. In short, wherever he went he would have the assailants behind him; and these light-armed assailants were the most awkward of all—their arrows, darts, stones, and slings making them formidable at a distance, with no way of getting at them at close quarters, since they could conquer in flight, and the moment their pursuer turned they were upon him. Such was the idea that inspired Demosthenes in his conception of the descent, and that presided over its execution.

Meanwhile the main body of the troops on the island (those under Epitadas), seeing their outpost cut off and an army advancing against them, closed ranks and pressed forward to engage the Athenian heavy infantry in front of them, the light troops being on their flanks and rear. They were unable, however, either to engage or to make use of their superior skill, since the light troops kept them in check on either side with their missiles, and the heavy infantry remained stationary instead of advancing to meet them. Although they routed the light troops wherever they ran up and approached too closely, they retreated fighting, being lightly equipped and easily getting the start in flight, given the difficult and rugged ground of an island that had until then been deserted, over which the Lacedaemonians could not pursue them in their heavy armour.

After this skirmishing had gone on for a little while, the Lacedaemonians became unable to dash out with the same speed as before at the points attacked, and the light troops, seeing that they now fought with less vigour, became more confident. They could see with their own eyes that they were many times more numerous than the enemy; they were now more familiar with his look, and found him less terrible, since the result had not justified the apprehensions they had felt when they first landed in slavish dismay at the idea of attacking Lacedaemonians. Their fear changing to disdain, they now rushed all together with loud shouts upon them, pelting them with stones, darts, and arrows—whatever came first to hand. The shouting accompanying their onset confounded the Lacedaemonians, who were unaccustomed to this style of fighting; dust rose from the newly burnt wood, and it was impossible to see in front of one with the arrows and stones flying through clouds of dust from the hands of numerous assailants. The Lacedaemonians had now to endure a rude conflict; their caps would not keep out the arrows; darts had broken off in the armour of the wounded; while they themselves were helpless for offence, prevented from using their eyes to see what was in front of them, and unable to hear the words of command for the hubbub raised by the enemy. Danger encompassed them on every side, and there was no hope of any means of defence or safety.

At last, after many had already been wounded in the confined space in which they were fighting, they formed up in close order and retired on the fort at the end of the island, which was not far off, and to their friends who held it. The moment they gave way, the light troops became bolder and pressed on them, shouting louder than ever, and killing as many as they came up with in their retreat. Most of the Lacedaemonians, however, made good their escape to the fort, and with the garrison there ranged themselves all along its whole extent to repulse the enemy wherever it could be assailed. The Athenians, in pursuit, unable to surround and hem them in because of the strength of the ground, attacked them in front and tried to storm the position. For a long time, indeed for most of the day, both sides held out against all the torments of the battle, thirst, and sun, the one trying to drive the enemy from the high ground, the other to maintain himself on it. It was now easier for the Lacedaemonians to defend themselves than before, since they could no longer be surrounded on the flanks.

The struggle began to seem endless, when the commander of the Messenians came to Cleon and Demosthenes and told them they were wasting their efforts; but if they would give him some archers and light troops to go round to the enemy’s rear by a way he would undertake to find, he thought he could force the approach. On receiving what he asked for, he started from a point out of sight to avoid being seen by the enemy, and creeping on wherever the precipices of the island allowed, and where the Lacedaemonians, trusting to the strength of the ground, kept no guard, succeeded after the greatest difficulty in getting round without being seen, and suddenly appeared on the high ground in their rear, to the dismay of the surprised enemy and the still greater joy of his expectant friends. The Lacedaemonians, thus placed between two fires, in the same dilemma—to compare small things with great—as at Thermopylae, where the defenders were cut off through the Persians getting round by the path, being now attacked in front and behind, began to give way. Overcome by the odds against them and exhausted from want of food, they retreated.

The Athenians were already masters of the approaches when Cleon and Demosthenes, perceiving that if the enemy gave way a single step further they would be destroyed by their soldiery, put a stop to the battle and held their men back. They wished to take the Lacedaemonians alive to Athens, hoping that their stubbornness might relax on hearing the offer of terms, and that they might surrender and yield to the present overwhelming danger. Proclamation was accordingly made to ask if they would surrender themselves and their arms to the Athenians, to be dealt with at their discretion.

Hearing this offer, most of the Lacedaemonians lowered their shields and waved their hands to show that they accepted it. Hostilities now ceased, and a parley was held between Cleon and Demosthenes on one side, and Styphon, son of Pharax, on the other; for Epitadas, the first of the previous commanders, had been killed, and Hippagretas, the next in command, left for dead among the slain (though still alive), and so the command had devolved on Styphon according to the law, in case anything happened to his superiors. Styphon and his companions said they wished to send a herald to the Lacedaemonians on the mainland, to know what they were to do. The Athenians would not let any of them go, but themselves called for heralds from the mainland, and after questions had been carried back and forth two or three times, the last man to come over from the Lacedaemonians on the continent brought this message: “The Lacedaemonians bid you decide for yourselves, so long as you do nothing dishonourable.” On this, after consulting together, they surrendered themselves and their arms. The Athenians, after guarding them that day and night, the next morning set up a trophy on the island and got ready to sail, handing their prisoners in batches to be guarded by the captains of the galleys; and the Lacedaemonians sent a herald and took up their dead. The number of the killed and prisoners taken on the island was as follows: four hundred and twenty heavy infantry had crossed over; three hundred all but eight were taken alive to Athens; the rest were killed. About a hundred and twenty of the prisoners were Spartans. The Athenian loss was small, since the battle had not been fought at close quarters.

The blockade altogether, counting from the sea-fight to the battle on the island, had lasted seventy-two days. For twenty of these, during the absence of the envoys sent to negotiate peace, the men had provisions given to them; for the rest they were fed by the smugglers. Corn and other food were found on the island; the commander Epitadas had kept the men on half rations. The Athenians and Peloponnesians now each withdrew their forces from Pylos and went home; and crazy as Cleon’s promise was, he fulfilled it by bringing the men to Athens within the twenty days as he had pledged.

Nothing that happened in the war surprised the Hellenes so much as this. The opinion was that no force or famine could make the Lacedaemonians give up their arms, but that they would fight on as best they could and die with their weapons in their hands. Indeed people could scarcely believe that those who had surrendered were of the same stuff as the fallen. An Athenian ally, who some time later insultingly asked one of the prisoners from the island whether those who had fallen were men of honour, received for answer that the atraktos—that is, the arrow—would be worth a great deal if it could tell men of honour from the rest; an allusion to the fact that the killed were those whom the stones and the arrows happened to hit.

On the arrival of the men, the Athenians decided to keep them in prison until the peace, and if the Peloponnesians invaded their country in the interval, to bring them out and put them to death. Meanwhile the defence of Pylos was not forgotten. The Messenians from Naupactus sent to their old country, to which Pylos had once belonged, some of the likeliest of their number, and began a series of incursions into Laconia, which their common dialect made all the more destructive. The Lacedaemonians, until then without experience of incursions or warfare of this kind, finding the Helots deserting and fearing the march of revolution in their country, began to grow seriously uneasy. Despite their unwillingness to betray this to the Athenians, they began to send envoys to Athens, and tried to recover Pylos and the prisoners. The Athenians, however, kept grasping at more, and dismissed envoy after envoy without their having achieved anything. Such was the history of the affair of Pylos.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 13 — Seventh and Eighth Years of the War—End of Corcyraean Revolution— Peace of Gela—Capture of Nisaea
paragraphs: The same summer, immediately after these events, the Athenians made an expedition against the territory of Corinth with eighty ships and two thousand Athenian heavy infantry, and two hundred cavalry on board horse transports, accompanied by the Milesians, Andrians, and Carystians from the allies, under the command of Nicias, son of Niceratus, with two colleagues. Putting out to sea, they made land at daybreak between Chersonese and Rheitus, on the beach of the country beneath the Solygian hill—where the Dorians in old times had established themselves and made war on the Aeolian inhabitants of Corinth, and where a village now stands called Solygia. The beach where the fleet came in is about a mile and a half from the village, seven miles from Corinth, and two and a quarter from the Isthmus. The Corinthians had heard from Argos of the coming of the Athenian armament, and had all come up to the Isthmus long before, except those who lived beyond it, and five hundred who were away on garrison duty in Ambracia and Leucadia; and they were there in full force watching for the Athenians to land. The Athenians, however, gave them the slip by coming in the dark; and the Corinthians, informed by signals of the fact, left half their number at Cenchreae, in case the Athenians should march on Crommyon, and themselves marched in all haste to the rescue.

Battus, one of the two generals present at the action, went with a company to defend the village of Solygia, which was unfortified; Lycophron remained to give battle with the rest. The Corinthians first attacked the right wing of the Athenians, which had just landed in front of Chersonese, and afterwards the rest of the army. The battle was a stubborn one, fought throughout hand to hand. The right wing of the Athenians and Carystians, who had been placed at the end of the line, received the Corinthians and with some difficulty repulsed them. The Corinthians then retreated to a wall on the rising ground behind, and throwing down stones at them, came on again singing the paean. Received once more by the Athenians, they engaged at close quarters again. At this moment a Corinthian company that had come to the relief of the left wing routed and pursued the Athenian right to the sea, where they were in turn driven back by the Athenians and Carystians from the ships. Meanwhile the rest of the army on each side fought on tenaciously, especially the right wing of the Corinthians, where Lycophron sustained the attack of the Athenian left, which it was feared might attempt the village of Solygia.

After holding on for a long time without either side giving way, the Athenians, aided by their cavalry—of which the enemy had none—at last routed the Corinthians, who retired to the hill, halted, and remained quiet there, not coming down again. It was in this rout of the right wing that they had the most killed, Lycophron their general being among them. The rest of the army, broken and put to flight in this way without being seriously pursued or hurried, retired to the high ground and took up its position there. The Athenians, finding that the enemy no longer offered to engage them, stripped his dead and took up their own and at once set up a trophy. Meanwhile, the half of the Corinthians left at Cenchreae to guard against the Athenians sailing on Crommyon, although unable to see the battle on account of Mount Oneion, found out what was going on by the dust, and hurried up to the rescue; as did the older Corinthians from the town, when they heard what had happened. The Athenians, seeing them all coming against them, and thinking they were reinforcements arriving from the neighbouring Peloponnesians, withdrew in haste to their ships with their spoils and their own dead—except two whom they left behind, not being able to find them—and going on board crossed over to the islands opposite. From there they sent a herald and took up under truce the bodies they had left behind. Two hundred and twelve Corinthians fell in the battle, and rather less than fifty Athenians.

Weighing anchor from the islands, the Athenians sailed the same day to Crommyon in Corinthian territory, about thirteen miles from the city, and coming to anchor laid waste the country and spent the night there. The next day, after first coasting along to the territory of Epidaurus and making a descent there, they came to Methana between Epidaurus and Troezen. They drew a wall across and fortified the isthmus of the peninsula, and left a post there, from which raids were thereafter made on the country of Troezen, Haliae, and Epidaurus. After walling off this spot, the fleet sailed off home.

While these events were going on, Eurymedon and Sophocles had put to sea with the Athenian fleet from Pylos on their way to Sicily. On arriving at Corcyra, they joined the townsmen in an expedition against the party established on Mount Istone, who had crossed over, as I have mentioned, after the revolution and become masters of the country, to the great hurt of the inhabitants. Their stronghold was taken by an attack, and the garrison took refuge in a body on some high ground, where they capitulated, agreeing to give up their mercenary auxiliaries, lay down their arms, and commit themselves to the discretion of the Athenian people. The generals carried them across under truce to the island of Ptychia, to be held until they could be sent to Athens, on the understanding that if any were caught running away, all would lose the benefit of the treaty. Meanwhile the leaders of the Corcyraean commons, afraid that the Athenians might spare the prisoners’ lives, resorted to the following stratagem. They won over a few of the men on the island by secretly sending friends with instructions to provide them with a boat, and to tell them—as if for their own sakes—that they had best escape as quickly as possible, since the Athenian generals were going to hand them over to the Corcyraean people.

These representations succeeded, and it was so arranged that the men were caught sailing out in the boat that had been provided. The treaty thus became void, and the whole body was handed over to the Corcyraeans. For this result the Athenian generals were largely responsible: their evident reluctance to sail for Sicily, and so to leave to others the honour of conducting the men to Athens, encouraged the intriguers in their design and seemed to confirm the truth of their representations. The prisoners thus handed over were shut up by the Corcyraeans in a large building, and afterwards taken out by twenties and led between two lines of heavy infantry, one on each side, bound together, and beaten and stabbed by the men in the lines whenever any saw a personal enemy go past; while men carrying whips walked alongside and hurried on those who walked too slowly.

As many as sixty men were taken out and killed in this way without the knowledge of their friends in the building, who imagined they were merely being moved from one prison to another. At last, however, someone opened their eyes to the truth, and they called on the Athenians to kill them themselves, if such was their pleasure, and refused any longer to leave the building, saying they would do all they could to prevent anyone coming in. The Corcyraeans, not wanting to force a passage by the doors themselves, climbed onto the roof of the building, broke through it, and threw down the tiles and shot arrows at them; the prisoners sheltered themselves as well as they could. Most of them, meanwhile, were busy dispatching themselves—thrusting into their throats the arrows shot by the enemy, hanging themselves with cords taken from some beds that happened to be there, and with strips made from their clothing—adopting, in short, every possible means of self-destruction, and also falling victim to the missiles of their enemies on the roof. Night came on while these horrors were unfolding, and most of it had passed before they ended. When day came, the Corcyraeans threw the bodies in layers onto wagons and carried them out of the city. All the women taken in the stronghold were sold as slaves. In this way the Corcyraeans of the mountain were destroyed by the commons; and so, after terrible excesses, the party strife came to an end, at least as far as the period of this war is concerned, since of one party there was practically nothing left. Meanwhile the Athenians sailed off to Sicily, their primary destination, and carried on the war with their allies there.

At the close of the summer, the Athenians at Naupactus and the Acarnanians made an expedition against Anactorium, the Corinthian town lying at the mouth of the Ambracian Gulf, and took it by treachery; and the Acarnanians themselves, sending settlers from all parts of Acarnania, occupied the place.

Summer was now over. During the following winter, Aristides, son of Archippus, one of the commanders of the Athenian ships sent to collect money from the allies, arrested at Eion on the Strymon, Artaphernes, a Persian, on his way from the King to Lacedaemon. He was conducted to Athens, where the Athenians had his dispatches translated from the Assyrian script and read them. With many references to other matters, they essentially told the Lacedaemonians that the King did not know what they wanted, since of the many ambassadors they had sent him no two ever told the same story; if, however, they were willing to speak plainly, they should send him some envoys with this Persian. The Athenians afterwards sent Artaphernes back in a galley to Ephesus, and ambassadors with him, who there learned of the death of King Artaxerxes, son of Xerxes, which took place about that time, and so returned home.

The same winter the Chians pulled down their new wall on the orders of the Athenians, who suspected them of plotting an insurrection, having first, however, obtained pledges from the Athenians and as much security as possible that they would continue to be treated as before. Thus the winter ended, and with it ended the seventh year of the war that Thucydides is the historian of.

In the first days of the next summer there was an eclipse of the sun at the time of new moon, and in the early part of the same month an earthquake. Meanwhile, the Mitylenian and other Lesbian exiles set out, mostly from the mainland, with mercenaries hired in the Peloponnese and others levied on the spot, and took Rhoeteum, but restored it without injury on receipt of two thousand Phocaean staters. After this they marched against Antandrus and took the town by treachery, their plan being to free Antandrus and the rest of the Actaean towns, formerly owned by Mitylene but now held by the Athenians. Once fortified there, they would have every facility for ship-building, given the proximity of Ida and the resulting abundance of timber, and plenty of other supplies; from this base they could easily ravage Lesbos, which was not far off, and make themselves masters of the Aeolian towns on the mainland.

While these were the schemes of the exiles, the Athenians the same summer made an expedition with sixty ships, two thousand heavy infantry, a few cavalry, and some allied troops from Miletus and other parts, against Cythera, under the command of Nicias, son of Niceratus, Nicostratus, son of Diotrephes, and Autocles, son of Tolmaeus. Cythera is an island lying off Laconia, opposite Malea; the inhabitants are Lacedaemonians of the Perioeci class, and an officer called the judge of Cythera went over to the place each year from Sparta. A garrison of heavy infantry was also regularly sent there, and great attention was paid to the island, since it was the landing place for merchantmen from Egypt and Libya, and at the same time secured Laconia from the attacks of privateers from the sea, at the only point where it is assailable, since the whole coast rises abruptly toward the Sicilian and Cretan seas.

Coming to land here with their armament, the Athenians, with ten ships and two thousand Milesian heavy infantry, took the town of Scandea on the sea; with the rest of their forces, landing on the side of the island facing Malea, they marched against the lower town of Cythera, where they found all the inhabitants encamped. A battle ensued, in which the Cytherians held their ground for a little while, then turned and fled into the upper town, where they soon afterwards capitulated to Nicias and his colleagues, agreeing to leave their fate to the decision of the Athenians, with only their lives guaranteed. A correspondence had previously been going on between Nicias and certain inhabitants, which made the surrender happen more quickly and on terms more advantageous, both for the present and the future, for the Cytherians, who would otherwise have been expelled by the Athenians on account of their being Lacedaemonians and their island being so near to Laconia. After the capitulation, the Athenians occupied the town of Scandea near the harbour, and appointing a garrison for Cythera, sailed to Asine, Helus, and most of the places on the sea, making descents and spending the night ashore wherever convenient, and continued ravaging the country for about seven days.

The Lacedaemonians, seeing the Athenians masters of Cythera, and expecting descents of the same kind on their own coasts, did not oppose them in force anywhere. They sent garrisons here and there throughout the country, consisting of as many heavy infantry as the points threatened seemed to require, and generally stood very much on the defensive. After the severe and unexpected blow they had suffered on the island, the occupation of Pylos and Cythera, and the apparition on every side of a war whose rapidity defied precaution, they lived in constant fear of internal revolution, and now took the unusual step of raising four hundred horse and a force of archers. They became more timid than ever in military matters, finding themselves caught in a maritime struggle their organisation had never contemplated, and that against Athenians, with whom an enterprise unattempted was always looked on as a success sacrificed. Besides this, their recent numerous reverses of fortune, coming close one upon another without any reason, had thoroughly unnerved them. They were always afraid of a second disaster like the one on the island, and so scarcely dared to take the field, but fancied that they could not stir without making a blunder; for being new to the experience of adversity, they had lost all confidence in themselves.

Accordingly they now allowed the Athenians to ravage their seaboard without making any move, the garrisons in whose neighbourhood the descents were made always thinking their numbers insufficient, and sharing the general feeling. A single garrison that ventured to resist, near Cotyrta and Aphrodisia, struck terror by its charge into the scattered mob of light troops, but retreated, on being received by the heavy infantry, with the loss of a few men and some arms; for which the Athenians set up a trophy, and then sailed off to Cythera. From there they sailed round to Epidaurus Limera, ravaged part of the country, and so came to Thyrea in the Cynurian territory, on the Argive and Laconian border. This district had been given by its Lacedaemonian owners to the expelled Aeginetans to live in, in return for their good offices at the time of the earthquake and the rising of the Helots, and also because, although subjects of Athens, they had always sided with Lacedaemon.

While the Athenians were still at sea, the Aeginetans evacuated a fort they were building on the coast and retreated into the upper town where they lived, rather more than a mile from the sea. One of the Lacedaemonian district garrisons, which was helping them in the work, refused to enter here with them at their entreaty, thinking it dangerous to shut themselves up within the wall, and retired to the high ground where they remained quiet, not considering themselves a match for the enemy. Meanwhile the Athenians landed and at once advanced with all their forces and took Thyrea. The town they burnt, pillaging what was in it; the Aeginetans not killed in action they took with them to Athens, along with Tantalus, son of Patrocles, their Lacedaemonian commander, who had been wounded and taken prisoner. They also took with them a few men from Cythera whom they thought it safest to remove. The Athenians decided to lodge these in the islands; the rest of the Cytherians were to keep their lands and pay four talents tribute. The captured Aeginetans were all to be put to death, on account of the old inveterate feud, and Tantalus was to share the imprisonment of the Lacedaemonians taken on the island.

The same summer, the inhabitants of Camarina and Gela in Sicily first made an armistice with each other, after which embassies from all the other Sicilian cities assembled at Gela to try to bring about a pacification. After many expressions of opinion on one side and the other, according to the grievances and pretensions of the various complaining parties, Hermocrates, son of Hermon, a Syracusan, the most influential man among them, addressed the assembly with the following words:

“If I now address you, Sicilians, it is not because my city is the smallest in Sicily or the greatest sufferer by the war, but in order to state publicly what seems to me the best policy for the whole island. That war is an evil is a proposition so familiar to everyone that it would be tedious to develop it. No one is forced into it by ignorance, or kept out of it by fear, if he thinks there is anything to be gained by it. To the former, the gain seems greater than the danger; the latter would rather face the risk than put up with any immediate sacrifice. But if both happen to have chosen the wrong moment for acting in this way, advice to make peace would not be useless; and this, if we did but see it, is just what we stand most in need of at the present juncture.

“I suppose no one will dispute that we went to war originally to serve our several interests; that we are now, in view of the same interests, debating how we can make peace; and that if we separate without having, as we think, our rights, we shall go to war again. As men of sense, we ought to see that more than our separate interests is at stake at this congress: there is also the question whether we still have time to save Sicily, the whole of which, in my opinion, is threatened by Athenian ambition. We ought to find in the name of that people more compelling arguments for peace than any I can advance, when we see the first power in Hellas watching our mistakes with the few ships she has at present in our waters, and under the fair name of alliance speciously seeking to turn to her own account the natural hostility that exists between us. If we go to war and call in to help us a people that are ready enough to carry their arms even where they are not invited; and if we injure ourselves at our own expense and at the same time serve as the pioneers of their dominion, we may expect that, when they see us worn out, they will one day come with a larger armament and seek to bring us all into subjection.

“And yet as sensible men, if we call in allies and court danger, it should be in order to enrich our different countries with new acquisitions, not to ruin what they already possess. We should understand that the internal discords so fatal to communities generally will be equally so to Sicily, if we, its inhabitants, absorbed in our local quarrels, neglect the common enemy. These considerations should reconcile individual with individual, and city with city, and unite us in a common effort to save the whole of Sicily. No one should imagine that the Dorians alone are enemies of Athens, while the Chalcidian race is secured by its Ionian blood. The attack in question is not inspired by hatred of one of two nationalities, but by a desire for the good things in Sicily, the common property of us all. This is proved by the Athenian reception of the Chalcidian invitation: an ally that has never given them any assistance whatever immediately receives from them almost more than the treaty entitles him to. That the Athenians should cherish this ambition and practise this policy is very excusable; and I do not blame those who wish to rule, but those who are over-ready to serve. It is just as much in men’s nature to rule those who submit as it is to resist those who molest them; one is no less invariable than the other. Meanwhile all who see these dangers and refuse to provide for them properly, or who have come here without having made up their minds that our first duty is to unite to be rid of the common peril, are mistaken. The quickest way to be rid of it is to make peace with each other, since the Athenians are threatening us not from their own country, but from the country of those who invited them here. In this way, instead of war issuing in war, peace will quietly end our quarrels, and the guests who came here under fair pretences for bad ends will have good reason to leave without having attained them.

“So far as the Athenians are concerned, such are the great advantages proved inherent in a wise policy. Independently of this, in the face of the universal agreement that peace is the first of blessings, how can we refuse to make it among ourselves? Do you not think that the good you have, and the ills you complain of, would be better preserved and cured by quiet than by war? That peace has its honours and splendours of a less perilous kind, not to mention the numerous other blessings one might dilate on, alongside the no less numerous miseries of war? These considerations should teach you not to disregard my words, but rather to look in them, every one of you, for his own safety. If anyone here feels certain, either by right or by might, that he can achieve his object, let him not find this surprise too severe a disappointment. Let him remember that many before now have tried to chastise a wrongdoer, and failing to punish their enemy, have not even saved themselves; while many who have trusted in force to gain an advantage, instead of gaining anything more, have been doomed to lose what they had. Vengeance is not necessarily successful because a wrong has been done, nor is strength sure because it is confident. The incalculable element in the future exercises the widest influence, and is the most treacherous, and yet in fact the most useful of all things, since it frightens us all equally, and so makes us think before attacking each other.

“Let us therefore now allow the undefined fear of this unknown future, and the immediate terror of the Athenians’ presence, to produce their natural effect; let us consider any failure to carry out the programmes each of us may have sketched as sufficiently accounted for by these obstacles, and send the intruder away from the country. If everlasting peace among us is impossible, let us at least make a treaty for as long a term as possible, and put off our private differences to another day. In short, let us recognise that the adoption of my advice will leave us each citizens of a free state, and as such arbiters of our own destiny, able to return good or bad offices with equal effect; while its rejection will make us dependent on others, and so not only impotent to repel an insult, but on the most favourable supposition, friends to our worst enemies and at feud with our natural friends.

“For myself, although, as I said at the start, the representative of a great city, and able to think less of defending myself than of attacking others, I am prepared to concede something in view of these dangers. I am not inclined to ruin myself for the sake of hurting my enemies, nor so blinded by animosity as to think myself equally master of my own plans and of fortune, which I cannot command; but I am ready to give up anything in reason. I call on the rest of you to imitate my conduct of your own free will, without being forced into it by the enemy. There is no disgrace in connections giving way to one another—a Dorian to a Dorian, or a Chalcidian to his brethren; above and beyond this, we are neighbours, live in the same country, are girt by the same sea, and go by the same name of Sicilians. We shall go to war again, I suppose, when the time comes, and again make peace among ourselves by means of future congresses; but the foreign invader, if we are wise, will always find us united against him, since the hurt of one is the danger of all; and we shall never, in future, invite into the island either allies or mediators. By acting this way we shall at the present moment do for Sicily a double service, ridding her at once of the Athenians and of civil war, and in future shall live in freedom at home and be less menaced from abroad.”

Such were the words of Hermocrates. The Sicilians took his advice and came to an understanding among themselves to end the war, each keeping what they had—the Camarinaeans taking Morgantina at a price fixed to be paid to the Syracusans. The allies of the Athenians called in the officers in command and told them that they were going to make peace and that they would be included in the treaty. The generals consenting, the peace was concluded, and the Athenian fleet afterwards sailed away from Sicily. On their arrival at Athens, the Athenians banished Pythodorus and Sophocles, and fined Eurymedon, on the charge of having taken bribes to depart when they might have subdued Sicily. So thoroughly had the present prosperity persuaded the citizens that nothing could withstand them, and that they could achieve what was possible and impracticable alike, with means ample or inadequate, it mattered not. The secret of this was their general extraordinary success, which made them confuse their strength with their hopes.

The same summer the Megarians in the city, pressed by the hostilities of the Athenians, who invaded their country twice every year with all their forces, and harassed by the incursions of their own exiles at Pegae, who had been expelled in a revolution by the popular party, began to ask one another whether it would not be better to receive back their exiles, and free the town from one of its two scourges. The friends of the émigrés, perceiving the agitation, now more openly than before demanded the adoption of this proposal; and the leaders of the commons, seeing that the sufferings of the times had worn out the loyalty of their supporters, in their alarm entered into correspondence with the Athenian generals, Hippocrates, son of Ariphron, and Demosthenes, son of Alcisthenes, and resolved to betray the town, thinking this less dangerous to themselves than the return of the party they had banished. It was accordingly arranged that the Athenians should first take the long walls extending nearly a mile from the city to the port of Nisaea, to prevent the Peloponnesians from coming to the rescue from there, where they formed the sole garrison securing the loyalty of Megara; and that after this an attempt should be made to put into their hands the upper town, which it was thought would then come over with less difficulty.

The Athenians, after plans had been arranged between themselves and their correspondents on both words and actions, sailed by night to Minoa, the island off Megara, with six hundred heavy infantry under the command of Hippocrates, and took up position in a quarry not far off, from which bricks used to be taken for the walls; while Demosthenes, the other commander, with a detachment of Plataean light troops and another of Peripoli, placed himself in ambush in the precinct of Enyalius, which was still nearer. No one knew of it except those whose business it was to know that night. A little before daybreak, the traitors in Megara began to act. Every night for a long time back, under pretence of marauding, in order to have a means of opening the gates, they had been used—with the consent of the officer in command—to carry by night a sculling boat on a cart along the ditch to the sea, and so to sail out, bringing it back again before day on the cart, and taking it within the wall through the gates, in order, as they pretended, to baffle the Athenian blockade at Minoa, since no boat was to be seen in the harbour. On the present occasion the cart was already at the gates, which had been opened in the usual way for the boat, when the Athenians, with whom this had been concerted, saw it and ran at top speed from the ambush in order to reach the gates before they were shut again, and while the cart was still there to keep them from being closed; their Megarian accomplices at the same moment killing the guard at the gates. The first to run in was Demosthenes with his Plataeans and Peripoli, just where the trophy now stands; and he was no sooner inside the gates than the Plataeans engaged and defeated the nearest party of Peloponnesians, who had taken the alarm and come to the rescue, and secured the gates for the approaching Athenian heavy infantry.

After this, each of the Athenians, as fast as they entered, went against the wall. A few of the Peloponnesian garrison stood their ground at first and tried to repel the assault, and some of them were killed; but the main body took fright and fled, the night attack and the sight of the Megarian traitors in arms against them making them think that all Megara had gone over to the enemy. It so happened, too, that the Athenian herald of his own accord called out and invited any of the Megarians who wished to join the Athenian ranks; and as soon as the garrison heard this, they gave way, convinced that they were the victims of a concerted attack, and took refuge in Nisaea. By daybreak the walls were now taken, and the Megarians in the city were in great agitation. The men who had negotiated with the Athenians, supported by the rest of the popular party which was in on the plot, said that they ought to open the gates and march out to battle. It had been concerted between them that the Athenians should rush in the moment the gates were opened, while the conspirators were to be distinguished from the rest by being anointed with oil, and so to avoid being hurt. They could open the gates with more security, since four thousand Athenian heavy infantry from Eleusis, and six hundred horse, had marched all night, by agreement, and were now close at hand. The conspirators, all anointed and at their posts by the gates, were ready when one of their accomplices denounced the plot to the opposing party, who gathered together and came in a body, and roundly said that they must not march out—a thing they had never yet ventured on even when in greater force than at present—or wantonly compromise the safety of the town; and that if their advice was not heeded, the battle would have to be fought in Megara. For the rest, they gave no signs of their knowledge of the intrigue, but stoutly maintained that their advice was the best, and meanwhile kept close by and watched the gates, making it impossible for the conspirators to carry out their purpose.

The Athenian generals, seeing that some obstacle had arisen and that the capture of the town by force was no longer practicable, at once proceeded to invest Nisaea, thinking that if they could take it before relief arrived, the surrender of Megara would soon follow. Iron, stone-masons, and everything else required quickly arrived from Athens. Starting from the wall they occupied, the Athenians built from this point a cross-wall facing Megara down to the sea on either side of Nisaea; the ditch and the walls were divided among the army, with stones and bricks taken from the suburb, and the fruit-trees and timber cut down to make a palisade wherever this seemed necessary; the houses in the suburb, with the addition of battlements, sometimes also became part of the fortification. The work continued the whole of this day, and by the afternoon of the next the wall was almost complete, when the garrison in Nisaea, alarmed by the absolute lack of provisions—which they used to take in for the day from the upper town—not anticipating any speedy relief from the Peloponnesians, and supposing Megara to be hostile, capitulated to the Athenians on condition that they should give up their arms and each be ransomed for a stipulated sum; their Lacedaemonian commander, and any others of his countrymen in the place, being left to the discretion of the Athenians. On these conditions they surrendered and came out, and the Athenians broke down the long walls at the point where they joined Megara, took possession of Nisaea, and went on with their other preparations.

Just at this time the Lacedaemonian Brasidas, son of Tellis, happened to be in the neighbourhood of Sicyon and Corinth, getting ready an army for Thrace. As soon as he heard of the capture of the walls, fearing for the Peloponnesians in Nisaea and the safety of Megara, he sent to the Boeotians to meet him as quickly as possible at Tripodiscus, a village so called of the Megarid, under Mount Geraneia, and went himself with two thousand seven hundred Corinthian heavy infantry, four hundred Phliasians, six hundred Sicyonians, and such troops of his own as he had already levied, expecting to find Nisaea not yet taken. Hearing of its fall (he had marched out by night to Tripodiscus), he took three hundred picked men from the army, without waiting for his coming to be known, and came up to Megara unobserved by the Athenians, who were down by the sea, ostensibly—and really, if possible—to attempt Nisaea, but above all to get into Megara and secure the town. He accordingly invited the townspeople to admit his party, saying that he had hopes of recovering Nisaea.

However, one of the Megarian factions feared that he might expel them and restore the exiles; the other feared that the commons, apprehensive of this very danger, might fall upon them, and the city be destroyed by a battle within its gates under the eyes of the ambushed Athenians. He was accordingly refused admittance, both parties choosing to remain quiet and await events; each expecting a battle between the Athenians and the relieving army, and thinking it safer to see their friends victorious before declaring in their favour.

Unable to carry his point, Brasidas went back to the rest of the army. At daybreak the Boeotians joined him. Having decided to relieve Megara—whose danger they considered their own—even before hearing from Brasidas, they were already in full force at Plataea when his messenger arrived to spur their resolution. They at once sent on to him two thousand two hundred heavy infantry and six hundred horse, the main body returning home. The whole army thus assembled numbered six thousand heavy infantry. The Athenian heavy infantry were drawn up by Nisaea and the sea; but the light troops, scattered over the plain, were attacked by the Boeotian horse and driven to the sea, taken entirely by surprise—since on previous occasions no relief had ever come to the Megarians from any quarter. Here the Boeotians were in turn charged and engaged by the Athenian horse, and a cavalry action ensued which lasted a long time, and in which both parties claimed the victory. The Athenians killed and stripped the leader of the Boeotian horse and a few of his comrades who had charged right up to Nisaea, and remaining masters of the bodies, gave them back under truce and set up a trophy; but, regarding the action as a whole, the forces separated without either side having gained a decisive advantage, the Boeotians returning to their army and the Athenians to Nisaea.

After this, Brasidas and the army came nearer to the sea and to Megara, and taking up a convenient position, remained quiet in order of battle, expecting to be attacked by the Athenians, and knowing that the Megarians were waiting to see who would be the victor. This stance seemed to offer two advantages. Without taking the offensive or willingly provoking the hazards of battle, they openly showed their readiness to fight, and so, without bearing the burden of the day, would fairly reap its honours; while at the same time they effectively served their interests at Megara. Had they failed to show themselves, they would have had no chance, but would certainly have been counted as defeated and lost the town. As it was, the Athenians might possibly not be inclined to accept their challenge, and their object would be attained without fighting. And so it turned out. The Athenians formed up outside the long walls and, the enemy not attacking, remained motionless; their generals had decided that the risk was too unequal. Most of their objects had in fact already been attained; they would have to begin a battle against superior numbers, and if victorious could only gain Megara, while a defeat would destroy the flower of their heavy soldiery. For the enemy it was different; even the states actually represented in his army each risked only a portion of its entire force, and so he might well be more daring. Accordingly, after waiting for some time without either side attacking, the Athenians withdrew to Nisaea, and the Peloponnesians after them to the point from which they had set out. The friends of the Megarian exiles now threw aside their hesitation and opened the gates to Brasidas and the commanders from the various states—looking on him as the victor and on the Athenians as having declined the battle—and receiving them into the town proceeded to discuss matters with them; the party in correspondence with the Athenians being paralysed by the turn things had taken.

Afterwards Brasidas let the allies go home, and himself went back to Corinth to prepare for his expedition to Thrace, his original destination. The Athenians also returned home; the Megarians in the city most implicated in the negotiations with Athens, knowing they had been detected, presently disappeared. The rest conferred with the friends of the exiles and restored the party at Pegae, after binding them under solemn oaths to take no vengeance for the past and to consult only the real interests of the town. As soon as they were in office, however, they held a review of the heavy infantry, and, separating the battalions, picked out about a hundred of their enemies, and of those thought to be most involved in the correspondence with the Athenians, brought them before the people, and compelling the vote to be given openly, had them condemned and executed, and established a close oligarchy in the town—a revolution which lasted a very long time, although effected by very few partisans.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 14 — Eighth and Ninth Years of the War—Invasion of Boeotia—Fall of Amphipolis—Brilliant Successes of Brasidas
paragraphs: That same summer the Mitylenians were about to fortify Antandrus, as they had intended, when Demodocus and Aristides, the commanders of the Athenian squadron engaged in collecting subsidies, heard on the Hellespont of what was being done to the place (Lamachus, their colleague, having sailed with ten ships into the Pontus). They feared it might become a second Anaia — the place where the Samian exiles had established themselves to harass Samos, helping the Peloponnesians by sending pilots to their navy, keeping the city in agitation, and receiving all its outlaws. They accordingly gathered a force from the allies, set sail, defeated in battle the troops that came out from Antandrus to meet them, and retook the place. Not long after, Lamachus, who had sailed into the Pontus, lost his ships at anchor in the river Calex in the territory of Heraclea, when rain that had fallen in the interior brought a flood suddenly down on them; and he and his troops marched overland through the Bithynian Thracians on the Asiatic side, and arrived at Chalcedon, the Megarian colony at the mouth of the Pontus.

That same summer the Athenian general Demosthenes arrived at Naupactus with forty ships, immediately after the return from the Megarid. He and Hippocrates had had overtures from certain men in the cities of Boeotia who wanted to change the constitution and bring in democracy as at Athens, the chief mover in this intrigue being Ptoeodorus, a Theban exile. The seaport town of Siphae, in the bay of Crisae in Thespian territory, was to be betrayed to them by one party; Chaeronea (a dependency of what was formerly called the Minyan, now the Boeotian, Orchomenus) was to be put into their hands by another from that town, whose exiles were very active in the business, hiring men in the Peloponnese. Some Phocians were also in the plot, since Chaeronea was the frontier town of Boeotia and close to Phanotis in Phocia. Meanwhile the Athenians were to seize Delium, the sanctuary of Apollo, in the territory of Tanagra facing Euboea; and all these events were to take place at the same time on an appointed day, so that the Boeotians would be unable to unite to oppose them at Delium, since they would be detained everywhere by disturbances at home. Should the enterprise succeed, and Delium be fortified, its authors confidently expected that even if no revolution immediately followed in Boeotia, yet with these places in their hands, the country harassed by raids, and a refuge close at hand for the partisans engaged in them, things would not stay as they were; and that with the rebels supported by the Athenians and the forces of the oligarchs divided, it would be possible after a while to settle matters as they wished.

Such was the plot in contemplation. Hippocrates, with a force raised at home, waited for the right moment to take the field against the Boeotians, while he sent on Demosthenes with the forty ships mentioned above to Naupactus, to raise an army in those parts from the Acarnanians and the other allies, and to sail and receive Siphae from the conspirators; a day having been agreed for the simultaneous execution of both operations. On his arrival, Demosthenes found that Oeniadae had already been compelled by the united Acarnanians to join the Athenian confederacy. He himself raised all the allies in those countries and marched against and subdued Salynthius and the Agraeans; after which he turned to the preparations needed to enable him to be at Siphae by the appointed time.

About the same time in the summer, Brasidas set out on his march for the Thracian towns with seventeen hundred heavy infantry, and on arriving at Heraclea in Trachis sent on a messenger to his friends at Pharsalus, asking them to escort him and his army through the country. Accordingly there came to Melitia in Achaia: Panaerus, Dorus, Hippolochidas, Torylaus, and Strophacus, the Chalcidian proxenus, under whose escort he resumed his march, accompanied also by other Thessalians, including Niconidas of Larissa, a friend of Perdiccas. It was never very easy to traverse Thessaly without an escort; and throughout Hellas, for an armed force to pass without leave through a neighbour's country was a delicate step. Besides this, the Thessalian people had always sympathized with the Athenians; indeed, if Thessaly had had a constitutional government instead of its customary close oligarchy, he would never have been able to proceed. Even as it was, he was met on his march at the river Enipeus by certain men of the opposite party, who forbade him to go further and complained that he was making the attempt without the consent of the nation. To this his escort answered that they had no intention of taking him through against their will: they were only friends in attendance on an unexpected visitor. Brasidas himself added that he came as a friend to Thessaly and its inhabitants, his arms being directed not against them but against the Athenians, with whom he was at war; and that although he knew of no quarrel between the Thessalians and Lacedaemonians that should prevent the two nations from having access to each other's territory, he neither would nor could proceed against their wishes — he could only beg them not to stop him. With this answer they went away, and he took the advice of his escort and pushed on without halting, before a greater force could gather to prevent him. Thus, on the day he set out from Melitia, he covered the whole distance to Pharsalus and encamped on the river Apidanus; and from there to Phacium, and from there to Perrhaebia. Here his Thessalian escort turned back, and the Perrhaebians, who are subjects of Thessaly, set him down at Dium in the dominions of Perdiccas, a Macedonian town under Mount Olympus, looking toward Thessaly.

In this way Brasidas hurried through Thessaly before anyone could get ready to stop him, and reached Perdiccas and Chalcidice. The departure of the army from the Peloponnese had been procured by the Thracian towns in revolt against Athens and by Perdiccas, alarmed at Athenian successes. The Chalcidians thought they would be the first targets of an Athenian expedition, though the neighbouring towns that had not yet revolted also secretly joined in the invitation; and Perdiccas, too, had his apprehensions because of his old quarrels with the Athenians, although he was not openly at war with them, and above all wished to reduce Arrhabaeus, king of the Lyncestians. It had been the easier to get an army to leave the Peloponnese because of the ill fortune of the Lacedaemonians at the moment. The Athenian attacks on the Peloponnese, and in particular on Laconia, might, it was hoped, be diverted most effectually by harassing them in return, and by sending an army to their allies — especially as the allies were willing to maintain it and asked for it to aid them in revolting. The Lacedaemonians were also glad to have an excuse for sending some of the Helots out of the country, for fear that the present state of affairs and the occupation of Pylos might encourage them to move. Indeed, fear of their numbers and stubbornness even drove the Lacedaemonians to the action I shall now describe, their policy at all times having been governed by the need to take precautions against them. The Helots were invited by a proclamation to pick out those of their number who claimed to have distinguished themselves most against the enemy, in order that they might receive their freedom; the real object being to test them, since it was thought that those most quick to claim their freedom would be the most high-spirited and the most likely to rebel. As many as two thousand were selected accordingly, who crowned themselves and went round the temples, rejoicing in their new freedom. The Spartans, however, soon afterwards did away with them, and no one ever knew how each of them perished. The Spartans now, therefore, gladly sent seven hundred as heavy infantry with Brasidas, who recruited the rest of his force by means of money in the Peloponnese.

Brasidas himself was sent out by the Lacedaemonians mainly at his own desire, although the Chalcidians, too, were eager to have a man as thorough as he had shown himself whenever there was anything to be done at Sparta, and whose subsequent service abroad proved of the utmost value to his country. At the present moment his just and moderate conduct toward the towns in general succeeded in bringing about their revolt, in addition to the places he managed to take by treachery; and so when the Lacedaemonians wished to come to terms, as they ultimately did, they had places to offer in exchange, and the burden of war was meanwhile shifted from the Peloponnese. Later in the war, after the events in Sicily, the valour and conduct of Brasidas — known by experience to some, by hearsay to others — was what mainly created among the allies of Athens a feeling for the Lacedaemonians. He was the first to go out and show himself so good a man at all points that he left behind him the conviction that the rest were like him.

Meanwhile, no sooner had his arrival in the Thracian country become known to the Athenians than they declared war on Perdiccas, whom they regarded as the author of the expedition, and kept a closer watch on their allies in that quarter.

On the arrival of Brasidas and his army, Perdiccas at once set out with them and his own forces against Arrhabaeus, son of Bromerus, king of the Lyncestian Macedonians, his neighbour, with whom he had a quarrel and whom he wanted to subdue. When, however, he arrived with his army and Brasidas at the pass leading into Lyncus, Brasidas told him that before opening hostilities he wished to go and try to persuade Arrhabaeus to become an ally of Lacedaemon. Arrhabaeus had already made overtures hinting at his willingness to make Brasidas arbitrator between them, and the Chalcidian envoys accompanying Brasidas had warned him not to relieve the apprehensions of Perdiccas, so as to keep him keener in their cause. Besides, the envoys of Perdiccas had spoken at Lacedaemon of his bringing many of the surrounding places into alliance with them, so Brasidas thought he might take a larger view of the question of Arrhabaeus. Perdiccas, however, retorted that he had not brought Brasidas with him to arbitrate his quarrel, but to put down the enemies he pointed out to him; and that while he, Perdiccas, was maintaining half the army, it was a breach of faith for Brasidas to parley with Arrhabaeus. Nevertheless, Brasidas disregarded Perdiccas's wishes and held the parley in spite of him, and let himself be persuaded to lead off the army without invading the country of Arrhabaeus; after which Perdiccas, judging that faith had not been kept with him, contributed only a third instead of half of the support of the army.

That same summer, without any loss of time, Brasidas marched with the Chalcidians against Acanthus, a colony of the Andrians, a little before vintage. The inhabitants were divided into two parties on the question of receiving him: those who had joined the Chalcidians in inviting him, and the popular party. However, fear for their fruit, which was still out, enabled Brasidas to persuade the multitude to admit him alone and hear what he had to say before deciding; and he was admitted accordingly and appeared before the people, and being not a bad speaker for a Lacedaemonian, addressed them as follows:

“Acanthians, the Lacedaemonians have sent me and my army out to make good the reason we gave for the war when we began it: that we were going to war with the Athenians in order to free Hellas. Our delay in coming has been caused by mistaken expectations as to the war at home, which led us to hope that by our own unassisted efforts and without any risk to you, we could effect the speedy downfall of the Athenians. You must not blame us for this, since we have come the moment we were able, prepared with your aid to do our best to subdue them. Meanwhile, I am astonished to find your gates shut against me, and to meet with no warmer welcome. We Lacedaemonians thought of you as allies eager to have us, to whom we should come in spirit even before we were with you in body; and in this expectation undertook all the risks of a march of many days through a strange country — so far did our zeal carry us. It will be a terrible thing if after this you have other intentions, and mean to stand in the way of your own and Hellenic freedom. It is not merely that you oppose me yourselves; but wherever I may go people will be less inclined to join me, on the ground that you, to whom I first came — an important town like Acanthus, and prudent men like the Acanthians — refused to admit me. I shall have nothing to prove that the reason I give is the true one; it will be said either that there is something unfair in the freedom I offer, or that I am in insufficient force and unable to protect you against an attack from Athens.
